If so, it might have been influenced by modify. Related: Transmogrified; transmogrifying; transmogrification (1660s).

Transylvania.x: region and former grand principality in the northern Balkans, incorporated into Hungary 1868, then part of Romania from after World War I; literally "beyond the forest," from Medieval Latin, from trans "beyond" (see trans-) + sylva (see sylvan). So called in reference to the wooded mountains that surround it. Related: Transylvanian.

tree-house.x: 1867, "house built in a tree," originally of native constructions in New Guinea; as a children's creation by 1949. See tree (n.) + house (n.).

tropho-.x: before vowels, troph-, word-forming element of Greek origin meaning "nourishment, food," from Greek trophē "nourishment" (see -trophy).

tropo-.x: word-forming element of Greek origin, used in sciences, etc., from late 19c. in a sense of "turning," from Greek tropos "a turn, change" (from PIE root *trep- "to turn").

tube-steak.x: "frankfurter," 1963, from tube (n.) + steak (n.). So called for its form. The slang meaning "penis" is recorded by mid-1980s.

turn-around.x:
also turnaround, by 1936, "arrival, unloading, loading, and departure of a ship, etc.," from verbal phrase turn around; see turn (v.) + around (adv.). The verbal phrase is from c. 1300 as "move in a circle, reverse position or course, return to a former position;" specifically by 1880 in American English transitively as "reverse."
As "reversal of a trend" by 1941 (British English preferred turn-round). As "place for vehicles to turn around" by 1954.

turn-off.x: "something that dampens one's spirits," by 1971 (said to have been in use since 1968), perhaps based on turn-on (v.). The verbal phrase turn off "stop the flow of" is attested from 1850; see turn (v.) + off (adv.). Earlier it meant "dismiss, send away" (1560s). Turn-off (n.) as "place where one road diverges from another" is from 1881; as "a causing to cease functioning" by 1967.

turn-out.x:
1680s, "action of coming forth," from the verbal phrase, which is attested by 1540s as "cause to go or come out;" see turn (v.) + out (adv.). Specifically as "audience, assemblage of persons who have come to see a show, spectacle, etc.," by 1816. To turn out "be ultimately" is attested by 1744.
As "labor strike," turn-out (n.) is attested from 1806; as "manner in which anything is equipped," by 1812. The verbal phrase is attested as "dismiss, eject" (from office, power, etc.) by 1580s; as "cause to stumble or roll away," late 14 c.

two-dimensional.x: 1883, "having length and breadth but no depth;" see two + dimension + -al (1). The figurative sense of "lacking substance or depth" is attested by 1934. Related: Two-dimensionality.

two-fisted.x: "sturdy, tough and aggressive," 1774, American English; see two + fist (n.). Earlier it meant "two-handed" (1680s).

two-time.x: "deceive, cheat, betray" in romance or courtship, 1924, perhaps from notion of "have two at a time" or "be of both sides at once." An earlier reference (1922) in a Kentucky criminal case involves a double-cross or betrayal without a romance angle. Related: two-timing (adj.); two-timer. Also compare double-cross.

tripartient.x: "dividing into three," said of a number, 1706, from tri- "three" + formation from past-participle stem of Latin partiri "to divide" (from pars "a part, piece, a share," from PIE root *pere- (2) "to grant, allot").

theregates.x: "in that way or manner," mid-15c., from there + -gates (compare allgates).

tenticle.x: "a little tent," 1540s, from Medieval Latin *tentacula, diminutive of tenta "tent" (see tent (n.)).

tabbouli.x: also tabouli, tabbouleh, Middle Eastern vegetable salad, 1937, from Arabic tabbula.

Thalidomide.x: non-barbiturate sedative used as a morning-sickness drug, 1958, from "phthalimidoglutarimide," based on abbreviated form of naphthalene. Responsible for severe birth defects in Europe from 1956 to 1961, when it was withdrawn. Never was approved for use in America due to the efforts of Dr. Helen Brooke Taussig (1898-1986) and others. Thalidomide baby is attested from 1962.

Tibert.x: the name of the cat in "Reynard the Fox" (late 15c., Caxton), hence an old proper name for any cat, from Flemish and Dutch Tybert, Old French Tibert. It was identified in Shakespeare with masc. proper name Tibalt, which is from Old French Thibauld, from Germanic *Theobald (see Theobald).

tried.x: "tested, proven, trusty," mid-14c., past-participle adjective from try (v.). It has been coupled alliteratively with true (adj.) since mid-14c. Also in Middle English "finely ground or sifted" (early 14c.); "purified, refined" (mid-14c.). Middle English also had triedly "excellently" (c. 1400).

typing.x: "action of typing," in any sense, 1630s, originally theological, verbal noun from type (v.).

teeming.x: "swarming," 1715, earlier "prolific, abundantly productive, fertile" (1590s), present-participle adjective from teem (v.1).

tracing.x: late 14c., "a drawing representing the structure of some object," verbal noun from trace (v.). Tracing-paper is attested by 1824.

tanling.x: "one scorched or tanned by the sun," 1610s, from tan (v.) + -ling.

teething.x: "dentition, the growth of teeth," 1724, verbal noun from teethe (v.). Teething-ring is attested from 1853. Earlier was toothing "the cutting of teeth" (mid-15c.).

teens.x: 1670s, "teen-age years of a person," from -teen taken as a separate word. As "numbers whose names end in -teen" by 1885, especially in reference to years of age; as "decade of years comprising numbers ending in -teen," by 1889.

threatening.x: 1520s, "portending no good; indicating or containing a threat," present-participle adjective from threat (v.). Related: Threateningly. In a Middle English glossary early 15c. Latin minax (adj.) is rendered by threati.

tired.x: "exhausted, fatigued, weary," early 15c., terede, past-participle adjective from tire (v.). As a nickname, Walter Teredlad is attested from 1301.

teaching.x: late Old English tecunge "act of providing guidance or training to another, imparting of instruction or knowledge," verbal noun from the source of teach (v.). Gradually passing into modern sense "business of instructing." As "that which is taught, knowledge or understanding imparted," it is attested from c. 1300. Middle English also had teachingless (adj.) "deprived of instruction, untaught" (mid-14c.).

topping.x:
"an act of putting a top on" anything, c. 1500, verbal noun from top (v.). The meaning "an act of cutting or pulling the top off" (a tree, plant, etc.) is from 1510s.
The sense of "that which is at or on the top of something" (hair, feathers, etc.) is from 14c. The meaning "top layer or garnish put on a food" is from 1839,

taps.x:
U.S. military signal for lights out in soldiers' quarters (played 15 minutes after tattoo), by 1824, from plural of tap (n.2), on the notion of drum taps (the call originally was played on a drum, later on a bugle).
As a soldier's last farewell, played over the grave, it may date to the American Civil War. The tune was revised several times in mid-19c.

touching.x: "moving, pathetic, affecting the emotions," a 16c. use of present-participle adjective from touch (v.), which is attested from 14c. as "affect or move mentally or emotionally." Related: Touchingly.

"concerning, in regard to, regarding," late 14c., from a special use of the present participle of touch (v.), on the model of French touchant, present participle of tochier. "Now somewhat arch." [OED, 1989]. Compare similar use of concerning. French touchant also was sometimes used in Middle English.

taws.x: also tawse, c. 1500, "whip for driving a spinning top," later also "leather thong slit in strips at the end," an instrument of school discipline, chiefly Scottish, of uncertain origin, perhaps from the notion of tawed leather (see taw (v.)).

tenderling.x: 1540s, "delicate or effeminate person;" 1580s, "young child;" see tender (adj.) + -ling.

tanning.x: late 15c., "process of tanning leather," verbal noun from tan (v.). The meaning "process of getting a sun-tan" is by 1944. Tanning booth is attested by 1978; tanning bed by 1981.

timing.x: mid-13c., "a happening, circumstance, occurrence," verbal noun from time (v.). It is attested from 1590s as "the noting or recording of time," and by 1915 as "coordination of moving parts in a machinery" so operation will follow in proper order.

tempting.x: "inviting, seductive, that entices or allures," 1540s to evil, 1590s to pleasure, present-participle adjective from tempt (v.). Other adjectives were temptative "inducing or leading to sin" (mid-15c., from Medieval Latin temptativus), temptatious (c. 1600), temptsome (1849). Related: Temptingly.

towards.x: Old English toweards, from toweard (adj.) "coming, facing, approaching" (see toward) + adverbial genitive ending.

telling.x: "effective, having effect or force," 1852, past-participle adjective from tell (v.).

transnihilation.x: "the transformation (of nothing) into nothings," 1820 (Coleridge, in a letter published 1836), see trans- + ending from annihilation.

Teletype.x: 1904, trademark for a system of typewriters connected electronically, short for teletypewriter (1904), a form of telegraph in which the receiver prints messages in the manner of a typewriter, from tele- + typewriter. As a verb by 1924.

thirties.x: 1827 as the years of someone's life between 30 and 39; attested by 1830 as "fourth decade of years in a given century." See thirty.

tractarian.x:
1824, "writer or publisher or distributor of tracts," from tract (n.2) + -arian. Tractator also was used for "writer of tracts."
Tractarian, with capital T-, as adjective and noun in reference to the High Churchmen who held the doctrines put forth by Newman (in "Tracts for the Times") is by 1840. Related: Tractarianism.

tapinage.x: "disguise, place of concealment, act of lurking" (obsolete), c. 1300, from Old French tapinage, from tapir "hide, skulk," a word of unknown origin. English also had tappish (v.) "to hide, take cover, lurk in a covert place," early 14c. (tapisen), from the present-participle stem of Old French tapir, which is said by the earlier French etymologists (Diez, Littré) to be from the same Germanic source as taper.

Teletex.x: proprietary name for a computer data-sharing network, 1978; see Telex + text.

tereu.x: representing a note of the nightingale, 1570s; it also is vocative of Tereus, the Thracian king who was the rapist of Philomela in the story (Ovid).

terms.x:
"propositions stated and offered for acceptance, limiting conditions," early 14c., from term (n.) in a sense of "stipulation, guarantee." Hence expressions such as come to terms "agree, yield;" make terms "come to an agreement;" on any terms, etc.
The meaning "standing, footing, mutual relations, relative position" is by 1540s, as in on good (or bad) terms (with someone); on speaking terms (1881).

Toussaint.x: French, literally "feast of All Saints" (Nov. 1), from tous, plural of tout "all" (from Latin totus; see total (adj.)) + saint "saint" (see saint (n.)).

trousers.x:
"garment for men, covering the lower body and each leg separately," 1610s, trossers, earlier trouzes (1580s), extended from trouse (1570s), with plural ending typical of things in pairs (tweezers), from Gaelic or Middle Irish triubhas "close-fitting shorts," a word of uncertain origin.
In early recorded use the garment was regarded as Celtic: "A jellous wife was like an Irish trouze, alwayes close to a mans tayle" [1630]. The unexplained, unetymological second -r- is perhaps by influence of drawers or other words in pairs ending in -ers. Also perhaps reinforced by truss (v.) in the sense "to dress." Related: Troused "wearing trousers" (1789).

traveled.x: "having made journeys, experienced in travel, having gained knowledge via travel," early 15c., past-participle adjective from travel (v.) Earlier it was "harassed, tormented" (late 13c.).

tempered.x: "brought to desired hardness" (of metals, especially steel), 1650s, past-participle adjective from temper (v.). The meaning "toned down by admixture" also is from 1650s. In modern use in reference to music or musical instruments, "tuned to a particular temper," from 1727 (compare well-tempered).

tops.x:
"the best," 1935, American English colloquial, from top (n.1), which is attested from 1660s as "highest example, type, or representation." Top (adj.) "prime, good, capital" was provincial English and Scottish in 19c.
It was short for top-boots from 16c.; also in various 19c. trade senses, such as "buttons plated on the showing side only" (as opposed to all-overs).

thews.x:
Old English þeawes "customs, habit, manners; morals, conduct, disposition, personal qualities," plural of þeaw "habit, custom," from Proto-Germanic *thawaz (source also of Old Saxon thau "usage, custom, habit," Old High German thau "discipline"). According to OED (1989), with no certain cognates outside West Germanic and of unknown origin.
The meaning "bodily powers or parts indicating strength, good physique" is attested from 1560s, from notion of "good qualities." Acquired a sense of "muscular development" when it was revived by Scott (1818).

taking.x: late 15c., "receiving," present-participle adjective from take (v.). By c. 1600 in the figurative sense of "captivating, attractive, pleasing." Related: Takingly. Colloquial taky "captivating, charming" is by 1854.

transmentation.x: "a change of mind," 1640s, from trans- "across, over" + Latin ment-, stem of mens "mind" (from PIE root *men- (1) "to think") + -ation.

trumper.x:
c. 1300, trompour, "a player on a horn or trumpet," from trump (v.) "sound a trumpet or horn," from trump (n.2) "trumpet." It is attested slightly earlier (mid-13c.) as a surname (Bartholomew le Trumpur; Matildis Trumpere). Also compare trumpeter. In modern political use, with capital T-, by 2015 as "follower or adherent of Donald Trump" (compare Trumpism).
From the source of trump (v.2) "fabricate, devise" came trumper as "deceiver, duper, hoaxer" (early 15c.), from Old French trompeur "deceiver," a variant of trompeor "trumpet-player" with an extended sense perhaps based on a now-obscure image. In Middle English glosses the word covers Latin tubicina, buccinator in the musical sense.

tedesco.x: "Teutonic influence in the arts," 1874 in this form (Byron, 1814, has Tedeschi), from Italian, literally "German," from Medieval Latin theodiscus (see Dutch). Compare Old French tiois "a German," tiesche (adj.) "German."

tumbester.x:
also tombester, "female acrobatic dancer or tumbler," late 14c., with fem. ending -ster + tumben "to leap, tumble dance; to fall," from Old English tumbian and Old French tomber (see tumble (v.)). Also tumblester (early 15c.).
 As the professional dancers of medieval times were usually also tumblers or acrobats, the words for dance and tumble were commonly used as synonymous. (Compare 
 hop, dance, 
 hopster, a female dancer, Latin 
 saltator, 
 saltatrix, a dancer, literally 'leaper.') The daughter of Herodias, who danced before Herod, is often pictured in medieval art as tumbling, walking on her hands, or standing on her head. [Century Dictionary]

twenties.x: 1829 as the years of someone's life between 20 and 29; 1830 as the third decade of years in a given century. See twenty.

transnivean.x: "beyond the snows," 1843; see trans- "beyond" + Latin nivem (nominative nix) "snow" (see neve) + -an. With reference to the geography and anthropology of India.

touched.x: past-participle adjective from the various senses of touch (v.). As "stirred emotionally," mid-14c.; as "sexually experienced," late 14c. As "impaired mentally in some slight degree" by 1704; elaborated form touched in the head for this is by 1902.

tarrying.x: "delaying, waiting, loitering," mid-14c., verbal noun from tarry (v.). Middle English also had tarriance (mid-15c.).

tumbling.x: late 14c., "dancing acrobatically; rolling about," verbal noun from tumble (v.).

thickening.x: early 15c., thikkening "thickener, substance used to thicken something," verbal noun from thicken (v.). Originally in cookery; by 1839 in reference to dyes and paints. By 1580s as "act or process of making thick or thicker."

taurian.x: "of or pertaining to a bull," 1882, from Latin taurus (see Taurus) + -ian. With capital T-, as "pertaining to the constellation Taurus," by 1909.

trunks.x: "short breeches of thin material," by 1825, from trunk (n.1) in the "torso" sense. Originally in theatrical jargon, the word was extended to breeches generally, especially in U.S. As short, tight-fitting breeches worn by swimmers and other athletes, by 1883.

tectonics.x: 1899 in the geological sense, "structural arrangement of the rocks of the planet's crust," from tectonic (also see -ics); earlier it meant "building or constructive arts in general" (1850).

thumping.x: "exceptionally large," colloquial, 1570s, present-participle adjective from thump (v.). Related: Thumpingly. Colloquial thumper "thing large and impressive of its sort" is by 1650s. For other examples, see strapping.

towering.x: c. 1600, figurative, "rising to a high pitch or intensity," present-participle adjective from tower (v.). The literal sense of "very high or lofty" is attested by 1630s. Related: Toweringly.

thanks.x:
mid-13c., plural of thank (n.) "expression of gratitude; kind feeling for another after a benefit received or service done," from Old English þanc, þonc in its secondary sense of "grateful thought, good will, gratitude." This is from the same Proto-Germanic root as thank (v.).
In prehistoric times the Germanic noun seems to have expanded from "a thinking of, a remembering" to also mean "remember fondly, think of with gratitude." Compare Old Saxon thank, Old Frisian thank, Old Norse þökk, Dutch dank, German Dank.
The Old English noun chiefly meant "thought, reflection, sentiment; mind, will, purpose," also "grace, mercy, pardon; pleasure, satisfaction," all now obsolete. The noun is used now exclusively in the plural.
Thanks as a common expression or acknowledgment (1580s) is short for I give you thanks, etc.; often with extensions, such as thanks a lot (1908). The form thanx is attested by 1888 as an illiterate spelling, by 1894 as a commercial or informal spelling.
 Thanx. That's one way to spell thanks. We are going to close our store from 11 o'clock to 2 oclock Thursday in order to have a short spell of thanx ourselves. [ad for The Mudge Mercantile Company, Eskridge (Kansas) Star, Thu., Nov. 26, 1896]

tickled.x: "pleased, happy," 1580s, figurative past-participle adjective from tickle (v.). To be tickled pink is from 1909.

tinned.x: "overlaid or plated with tin," past-participle adjective from tin (v.). As "packed or sealed in a tin container or containers," of fruits, meat, fish, etc., by 1861. Related: Untinned (1755).

Tib.x:
1530s, in 16c.-17c. a typical name for an English lass of the lower class, hence "girl, sweetheart," sometimes also "strumpet;" from the pet form of Isabel. She often was paired alliteratively with Tom, as Jill was with Jack. Also as a name for a female cat (tib-cat, 1828), perhaps by extension of the Tom pairing, but compare Tibert.
Colloquial St. Tibb's Eve (1785) was the evening of the last day, the Day of Judgment, hence "never."

tweedledum.x: paired with tweedledee to signify two things or persons nearly alike, differing in name, 1725, coined by English poet John Byrom (1692-1767) in his satire "On the Feud Between Handel and Bononcini," rival operatic composers in 1720s London, from tweedle "to sing, to whistle, play triflingly on a musical instrument" (1680s), a word of imitative origin. The -dum and -dee perhaps suggest low and high sounds respectively.

tweezers.x:
"small pincers; instrument resembling diminutive tongs intended for small objects, plucking hair, etc.," 1650s, extended from tweezes, plural of tweeze "case for tweezers" (1620s), a shortening of etweese, considered as plural of etwee (1610s) "a small case" (also tweeze "case of surgical instruments," 1620s), from French étui "small case" (see etui).
The sense was transferred from the case to the implement inside it. For form, compare trousers from trouzes. An earlier word for "tweezers, forceps" was twicches (plural), early 15c. in medical writing, related to twitch (v.) in its old sense of "to pluck."

toc.x: a word used for the letter -t- in radio communication to fill out and distinguish the letter, 1898. Compare ack (-a-), Emma (-m-). Toc H was British World War I colloquial for Talbot House, the behind-the-lines rest-house and club for soldiers.

toned.x: mid-15c. in reference to musical sound, past-participle adjective from tone (v.). By 1742 as "in a state of proper bodily firmness;" by 1864 of photographic positives, "tinted." With a specific qualifier (high-toned, etc.) by 1770s.

Torosaurus.x: dinosaur genus discovered in western U.S., 1891 (Marsh), from toro- "bull" (see toro) + -saurus. So called for its "horns."

trifling.x: "act or conduct of one who trifles, frivolous practice," late 14c., verbal noun from trifle (v.).

c. 1400, "cheating, feigning;" 1530s, "lacking depth or earnestness;" present-participle adjective from trifle (v.). In U.S. Southern colloquial, "good-for-nothing, worthless, low, mean." Triflous (c. 1500) also formerly was used.

tubing.x: recreational pastime of riding on a truck tire inner tube, by 1975 in reference to ski slopes, by 1976 in reference to rivers; see tube (n.).

tongued.x: in compounds and combinations, "speaking (in a certain manner)," late 14c. (double-tongued), from tongue (n.). Well-tongued (14c.) was "well-spoken."

tinning.x: mid-14c., "act, art, or process of plating metal surfaces with tin; a coating of tin," verbal noun from tin (v.). By 1903 as "the putting (of meat, fruit, etc.) in tins for preservation."

thereas.x: mid-14c., "there; where; in that place or case," from there + as.

trapping.x: "catching by snare or deceit," late 14c., verbal noun from trap (v.). As "the art, business, or methods of trappers," by c. 1600.
"cloth or covering spread over the saddle and harness of a horse," Middle English; see trappings.

tolling.x: c. 1200, "act of enticing or inciting;" c. 1300, "pulling, tugging;" mid-15c., "the sounding of a bell;" verbal noun from toll (v.).

thinking.x: "act of conceiving in the mind, the mental action of one who thinks, exercise of cogitation," mid-14c., verbal noun from think (v.). The figurative thinking cap is attested from 1839.

Thrasonical.x: "braggartly, given to boasting," 1560s from Thrasōn-, name of a braggart soldier in Terence's "Eunuchus"; the name is Greek, from thrasis "bold, spirited." Related: Thrasonically.

twinkling.x: c. 1300, "a wink, a glance," verbal noun from twinkle (v.). As "a shining, gleaming, flashing, sparkling," of fixed stars, etc., late 14c. Phrase in the twinkling of an eye "in a very brief time" is attested from c. 1300 (yn twynkelyng of an ye), also twink of an eye (c. 1400).

thriving.x: "prosperous, successful," especially in business, c. 1600, present-participle adjective from thrive (v.). Related: Thrivingly.

tigger.x: agent noun, "one who touches or pursues in the game of tig" (q.v., also known as tag), with -er (1), by 1893. To tig also was "touch playfully, tease and annoy by petty provocations."

trimming.x:
1510s, "preparation, a putting in order, a making trim," verbal noun from trim (v.). By 1530s as "dressing up." As "adjustment of a ship's balance, sails, etc.," by 1620s (see trim (n.)); figurative use of this is by 1690s. The earliest use is obsolete since early Middle English, "a spiritual strength or fortifying; an edifying matter," from Old English trymming.
Anything used for decoration or finish, hence trimmings, attested by 1610s as "adornments, accessories," in reference to dress or a house. It is attested by 1805 as "pieces cut off in scraps," a sense probably directly from the verb.

Thecodont.x: extinct reptile, 1840, so called for the tooth-sockets in the fossil jaws; from theco- "case, capsule" + -dont, from Greek odon (genitive odontos) "tooth" (from PIE root *dent- "tooth").

tendant.x:
mid-14c., tendaunt, "leading to a certain condition or state," from Old French tendant, past-participle of tendre "to offer, hold forth" (see tend (v.)).
The other Middle English tendaunt, "attentive, obedient" (late 14c.), is a shortening of attendant.

tables.x: "backgammon," late 13c., plural of table (n.). Plural in reference to the folding halves of the board.

tantalizing.x: "teasing or tormenting by offering something desirable but withholding it," by 1650s, present-participle adjective from tantalize. Tantalean in the same sense is from 1610s. Related: Tantalizingly.

traps.x: "drums, cymbals, bells, etc.," especially as extra equipment on a band drum set, 1925, from earlier trap drummer (1903) "street musician who plays a drum and several other instruments at once," perhaps from traps "belongings" (1813), shortened form of trappings.

trusting.x: mid-15c., "trustful, confiding" (implied in trustingly), present-participle adjective from trust (v.). Related: Trustingness.

trying.x: "distressing, hard to bear or endure, such as to test severely," 1718, present-participle adjective from try (v.) in the sense of "subject to strain." Related: Tryingly.

tights.x: 1827, "tight-fitting garments fitting closely to the legs," noun use of plural of tight (adj.). For the plural compare breeches. The meaning "skin-tights worn by dancers, acrobats, etc." to display form or facilitate movement is attested from 1836.

triangler.x: "triangle player in a band,"1840, agent noun from triangle (n.) in the percussion instrument sense.

theirs.x: possessive pronoun, "their own, their people, land, etc.," early 14c., from their + possessive -s, on analogy of his, hers, etc., but in form a double possessive. The same pattern happens in the earlier pronoun, native hiera, here "their;" attested by late Old English as heres.

tapetum.x: "pigmentary layer of the retina of the eye," 1713, from Medieval Latin tapetum, from Latin tapete, collateral form of tapes "carpet, heavy cloth with inwrought figures" (see tapestry). Related: Tapetal.

tyrannical.x: "acting like a tyrant, despotic in rule or behavior," 1530s, from Latin tyrannicus "arbitrary, despotic," from Greek tyrannikos "befitting a despot," from tyrannos (see tyrant) + -al (1). Caxton used tyrannic in this sense (late 15c.). From 1570s as "befitting a tyrant, oppressively harsh, cruel." Related: Tyrannically.

Turkophile.x: also Turcophile, 1876, from combining form of Turk + -phile.

tepee.x: tent used by some native North American peoples, 1743, ti pee, from Dakota (Siouan) thipi "dwelling, house."

turpentine.x:
early 14c., terbentyn, terebentine, "semi-liquid resin of the terebinth tree," from Old French terebinte "turpentine" (13c.), from Latin terebintha resina "resin of the terebinth tree," from Greek rhētinē terebinthē, from fem. of terebinthos (see terebinth).
By 16c. the word was applied generally to oleoresinous substances generated by the wood or bark of coniferous trees. Related: Turpentinic; turpentinous.

threadbare.x: late 14c., thred-bare, of garments, "worn-out, shabby," from thread (n.) + bare (adj.). The notion is of "having the nap worn off," leaving the foundation threads exposed. Figurative sense of "deficient" is by early 15c.

tortious.x: late 14c., torcious, "wrongful, illegal, injurious, harmful," from Anglo-French torcious (14c.), from stem of torcion, literally "a twisting," from Late Latin tortionem (see torsion, and compare tort). The meaning "pertaining to a tort" is from 1540s.

termite.x:
social insect noted for its destructiveness to timber, by 1794, a back-formation from termites (1781), three syllables, plural, and the usual early form of the word. It is from Modern Latin termites, plural of termes (genitive termitis), a special use of Late Latin termes "woodworm, white ant," a derivative of Latin terere "to rub, wear, erode" (from PIE root *tere- (1) "to rub, turn"), which altered its form.
A scientific name, they were known earlier in English as wood ant or white ant. Related: Termitic; termitine; termitologist. Their nest is a terminarium (1863).

teratogen.x: "agent or condition causing malformation of a developing embryo," 1959, from terato- "marvel, monster" + -gen "thing that produces or causes."

terbium.x: rare element, 1843, from Latinized form of Ytterby, Swedish town near the place where mineral containing the element was found (see Ytterbium). With metallic element ending -ium.

timbrel.x: percussive Middle Eastern instrument, mid-15c., diminutive of timbre (late 14c.), from Old French timbre in its older sense of "drum" (see timbre). It was used in Bible translations, chiefly to render Hebrew toph, cognate with Arabic duff "drum," ultimately of imitative origin.

trifocals.x: "glasses with trifocal lenses," 1899, from bifocals with tri-.

triannual.x: 1630s, "occurring every three years," from tri- + annual (adj.). By 1901 as "occurring three times a year." Related: Triannually. Compare triennial.

triable.x: early 15c., "capable of being tried in a court of law, subject to judicial determination;" from try (v.) + -able. By 1610s as "that may be tested or proven."

tucker.x: "piece of lace or other delicate fabric covering the neck and shoulders of a woman above the top of the bodice," 1680s, agent noun from tuck (v.). In Middle English tukere was "one who dresses or finishes cloth," hence the surname (mid-13c.), "one who stretches and fulls, a fuller."

"to tire, weary," 1833, New England colloquial, usually with out (adv.), of uncertain origin, perhaps from tucked (past participle of tuck (v.)), which had, in reference to dogs, a slang sense of "exhausted, underfed." Related: Tuckered; tuckering.

table-d'hote.x: "common table for guests at a hotel," French, table-d'hôte, "table of the host" (OED 2nd ed. print; Century Dictionary has it "table of the guest"); see table (n.) + host (n.).

table-land.x: a considerable region, elevated and generally level, 1690s, from table (n.) + land (n.). Table is attested from mid-15c. as "cleared, smoothed tract of land ready for planting."

tack-hammer.x: "small, light hammer used to drive tacks," often with a claw as well, for drawing them, 1848, from tack (n.1) + hammer (n.).

tail-coat.x: "coat with tails, coat with a divided skirt in back, swallow-tail coat," by 1847, from tail (n.1) + coat (n.).

tail-feather.x: "feather of a bird's tail," 1773, from tail (n.1) + feather (n.).

tail-fin.x: 1680s, "fin on the tail of a fish," from tail (n.1) + fin (n.). By 1940 in reference to aircraft; 1954 of automobiles.

tail-hook.x: 1861, in angling, "hook of a tail fly," from tail (n.1) + hook (n.).

tail-pipe.x: also tailpipe, 1757, "small pipe fixed at the swell of a musket to receive the ramrod," from tail (n.1) + pipe (n.). From 1832 as "suction pipe of a pump;" 1907 as "exhaust pipe at the rear of an automobile."

tail-race.x: 1776, "part of a mill race below the wheel," from tail (n.) in a specialized sense "slack part of a mill stream" (1530s) + race (n.3). Extended to hydroelectric dams by 1953.

tamper-proof.x: also tamperproof, "not susceptible to unauthorized changes," 1884, from tamper (v.) + proof. Originally of clocks that track workers' time on unsupervised duty.

tan-yard.x: also tanyard, 1712, "place where tanning is done;" see tan (v.) + yard (n.1).

tape-recorder.x:
"device for recording sound on magnetic tape," by 1932, from tape (n.) + recorder (n.1) "measuring apparatus." Earlier it meant "device for recording data on ticker tape" (1892), perhaps suggested by tape (n.) in an earlier mechanical sense in printing machines (by 1884).
Tape-record (v.) is attested from 1950. Tape-delay "interval between recording and playback" is attested by 1968. Tape deck (n.) is by 1949.

taste-bud.x: "one of the groups of cells on the tongue that perceive flavors," 1879; see taste (n.) + bud (n.). Related: Taste-buds. Also called taste-bulbs, taste-goblets.

Tay-Sachs.x: fatal inherited disorder, 1907, named in German (1901) by German neurologist Henryk Higier (1866-1942) from names of British ophthalmologist Warren Tay (1843-1927) and U.S. physician and neurologist Warren Sachs (1858-1944) who had independently described it in 1881 and 1887 respectively.

tea-ball.x: "wire ball in which loose tea is placed for infusion," 1895, from tea (n.) + ball (n.1).

tea-garden.x: "open-air enclosure attached to a house of entertainment, where tea is served," 1802, from tea + garden (n.). They were places of fashionable resort in 18c. England.

tea-room.x: "room in which tea is served," 1702, from tea + room (n.).

tea-rose.x: variety of rose having pale yellow flowers, 1825, from tea + rose (n.1); so called for its scent, supposed to resemble that of tea.

tea-spoon.x: also teaspoon, "small spoon, usually silver, for stirring tea in a cup," 1680s, from tea + spoon (n.). Related: teaspoonful.

tear-drop.x: also teardrop, "a tear," 1799, from tear (n.1) + drop (n.).

teeny-bopper.x: also teenybopper, "teenage or pre-teen girl," especially as a fan of pop music, 1966, from teen (n.) but also felt as influenced by teeny. For second element, see bop (v.).

tetaro-.x: word-forming element in science (crystallography) meaning "one-fourth, a quarter," from Greek tetaros "fourth," from tettares, tessares "four" (from PIE root *kwetwer- "four").

theco-.x: before vowels thec-, word-forming element of Greek origin used since 19c. in botany and zoology with a sense of "case, capsule;" from Latinized combining form of Greek thēkē "case, receptacle" (from suffixed form of PIE root *dhe- "to set, put"). Sometimes theci-, in Latinized form.

ther-.x: often thero-, word-forming element meaning "beast," from Greek thēr "wild beast, beast of prey" (from PIE root *ghwer- "wild beast"). Also therio-, theri-, from Greek thērion "wild animal, hunted animal," diminutive of thēr.

three-way.x: "having or going by three roads or channels, involving three ways," 1580s, from three + way (n.).

thumb-print.x: "mark or fingerprint left by a thumb," 1900, from thumb (n.) + print (n.). Thumb-mark is from 1845.

time-capsule.x:
1938, in reference to one "deemed capable of resisting the effects of time for five thousand years preserving an account of universal achievements" that was "embedded in the grounds of the New York World's fair." See time (n.) + capsule (n.). Considered by some at the time to be ballyhoo.
 Jones [archaeologist of A.D. 5139] potters about for a while in the region which we have come to regard as New York, finds countless ruins, but little of interest to the historian except a calcified direction sheet to something called a "Time Capsule." Jones finds the capsule but cannot open it, and decides, after considerable prying at the lid, that it is merely evidence of an archaic tribal ceremony called a "publicity gag" of which he has already found many examples. [Princeton Alumni Weekly, April 14, 1939]

time-span.x: also timespan, "a length or duration of time," during which something happens or between events, 1897, from time (n.) + span (n.1).

tin-type.x: also tintype, 1864 in photography, "positive image made on a thin plate of iron;" from tin + -type as in daguerreotype (q.v.). Not on your tintype was a U.S. colloquial dismissal ("certainly not!") attested by 1896 and popular c. 1900-1910.

tin-works.x: "establishment for the mining or manufacturing of tin," c. 1600, earlier tin-work (late 15c.); see tin (n.) + works.

tit-bit.x: also titbit, "delicate bit (of food), sweet morsel," 1630s; see tidbit.

to-go.x: in reference to food or beverage containers (often plastic) meant to be taken from the restaurant, 1987, from verbal phrase in ordering food; see to + go (v.).

toll-gate.x: also tollgate, "bar across a toll-road to block traffic until the toll is paid," 1773, from toll (n.) + gate (n.).

toll-house.x: also tollhouse, mid-14c. (late 13c. as a surname), "tollbooth, customs house," from toll (n.) + house (n.). Also compare tollbooth. Old English had toll-setle.

tom-fool.x: also tom-fool, "buffoon, clown, trifler," 1640s, from Middle English Thom Foole, a personification of or quasi-personal name for a mentally deficient man or a jester (mid-14c.), see Tom + fool (n.). By 18c. treated as an emphatic of fool.

tom-tom.x: "drum," 1690s, originally in an India context, in reference to the drum used by musicians, street entertainers, criers, etc. From Hindi tam-tam, which is probably of imitative origin (compare Sinhalese tamat tama and Malay tong-tong). Related: Tom-toms.

too-too.x: "excessive in social elegance," 1881, slang, from the emphatic reduplication of too (adv.).

tool-mark.x: "characteristic mark left on a surface shaped by a tool" (as on hewn timber, from a saw, plane, etc.), by 1865, from tool (n.) + mark (n.1).

tooth-ache.x: also toothache, "pain in the teeth" (formerly supposed to be caused by a worm), Old English toðece; see tooth (n.) + ache (n.).

top-castle.x: also topcastle, "platform at the top of a ship's mast," especially a fortified one on a fighting ship, early 14c.; see top (n.1) in the nautical sense + castle (n.) in the general Middle English sense of "any fortified place."

top-coat.x: 1804, "great coat, overcoat," from top (adj.) + coat (n.). By 1959 as "finishing coat of paint."

top-rail.x: nautical, "bar on stanchions extending across the after-part of a top," 1769, from top (n.1) + rail (n.1).

top-sail.x: also topsail, c. 1400, top-seile, "square sail set next above the lowest or chief sail of a mast;" see top (n.1) + sail (n.). Short form top is attested by 1510s.

top-sider.x: kind of casual shoe, 1937, from topside in nautical sense of "upper deck of a ship" (1670s), specifically "upper part of a ship's sides" (1815), where the rubber soles would grip; from top (n.1) + side (n.).

tort-feasor.x: also tortfeasor, in law, "wrongdoer, trespasser," literally "committer of a tort" in the old sense; 1650s, from Old French tortfesor, from tort "wrong, evil" (see tort) + -fesor "doer," from Latin facere "to make, do" (from PIE root *dhe- "to set, put").

touch-pad.x: in reference to a type of computer input device, 1980, from touch + pad (n.).

Touch-Tone.x: U.S. proprietary name for a push-button telephone apparatus, 1962, see touch + tone (n.).

tow-path.x: "path on the bank of a canal or river along which draft-animals travel in towing boats," 1788, from tow (v.) + path (n.).

toy-box.x: also toybox, "box for holding toys, box of toys," 1819, from toy (n.) + box (n.).

toy-maker.x: "maker or manufacturer of (children's) toys," 1859, from toy (n.) + maker. Earlier a maker of toys or keeper of a toy-shop might be a toyman (1707).

toy-shop.x: 1690s, "shop that sells trinkets and fancy articles;" 1796, "shop that sells children's playthings," from toy (n.) + shop (n.).

trade-name.x: "name invented or chosen as the specific designation of a commercial product," by 1821, from trade (n.) + name (n.). Compare trademark.

tragi-comedy.x: also tragicomedy, "dramatic composition characterized by both serious and comic scenes," 1570s, from French tragicomédie (1540s) or directly from Italian tragicommedia, from Late Latin tragicomoedia, contraction of tragicocomoedia (Plautus), from tragicus (see tragic) + comoedia (see comedy).

tragi-comic.x: "both serious and tragic, having both serious and comedic scenes," 1680s; see tragi-comedy + -ic. Related: Tragi-comical (1560s).

tragico-.x: word-forming element in classical form from Latinized form of Greek tragikos (see tragic).

train-oil.x: 1550s, "oil drawn, tried, or boiled out of the whale blubber," effectively right whale as opposed to sperm whale oil, from train (v.) in the old sense of "draw out and manipulate" + oil (n.).

train-spotting.x: 1959 (train-spotter attested from 1958), chiefly British English, in reference to the hobby of recording the numbers of railway locomotives one has observed; from train (n.) in the railroad sense + verbal noun from spot (v.).

tram-car.x: "conveyance used on a tram-way," originally especially a public horse-car on a street railway, by 1873; see tram + car (n.).

trans-oceanic.x: also transoceanic, by 1816, "existing or situated across the ocean," from trans- + oceanic. The meaning "passing over the sea" (in reference to flights of birds, ship-voyages) is recorded by 1859.

trash-man.x: also trashman, "one employed in the removal of rubbish and garbage," by 1892, from trash (n.) + man (n.). The older word was dustman (18c.) ; garbage collector is by 1872.

travois.x: type of Native American transport consisting of two long lodge-poles attached to the sides of a packsaddle with the ends trailing on the ground, 1847, earlier travail (1801), said to be ultimately from a Canadian indigenous pronunciation of French travail (see travail).

tree-frog.x: "frog of arboreal habits, batrachian which lives in trees," 1738, from tree (n.) + frog (n.1).

trench-coat.x: 1915, a type of waterproof coat worn by British officers in the trenches during World War I; see trench (n.) + coat (n.).

tri-dimensional.x: also tridimensional, "having three and only three dimensions," by 1836, in reference to space, in mathematical speculation; see tri- + dimension + -al (1).

tri-personal.x: also tripersonal, in a Christian context, "consisting of three persons," 1640s; see tri- + person + -al (1).

tricho-.x: before vowels trich-, word-forming element used from c. 1800 in botany, zoology, etc., and meaning "hair," from Greek trikho-, trikh-, combining forms of thrix (genitive trikhos) "hair," especially "body hair," as distinguished from komē, the well-groomed hair of the head. Beekes finds no cognates and gives it no etymology, noting, "The words for 'hair' are different in most Indo-European languages."

trigono-.x: word-forming element used in English in the sciences from late 18c., from Greek trigōnos "a triangle," noun use of adjective meaning "triangular, three-cornered;" from treis "three" (see tri-) + -gōnos "angled" (from PIE root *genu- (1) "knee; angle").

truck-lot.x: also trucklot, "amount of goods that would fill a truck," as a unit of sale, by 1943, from truck (n.1) + lot (n.).

truck-stop.x: "establishment along a highway for truckers to rest, eat, and refuel their engines," by 1956, from truck (n.1) + stop (n.).

true-love.x: Middle English treu-love "faithful love or its manifestation," from Old English treowlufu; see true (adj.) + love (n.). By late 14c. as "a faithful lover, sweetheart." True-love knot, a complicated knot as an ornamental symbol, is attested by late 15c.

tu-whit.x: paired with tu-whoo, imitative of the cry of the owl, 1580s.

tube-top.x: type of women's close-fitting elastic top, by 1972, from tube (n.) + top (n.); so called for its form.

tumble-bug.x: "type of beetle, dung-beetle," by 1805, from tumble (v.) + bug (n.). Also tumble-dung (1775), etc.; compare dung-beetle under dung.

tumble-down.x: 1791, of a horse, "habitually falling down," from tumble (v.) + down (adv.); in reference to buildings, "ruinous, in a dilapidated condition," from 1818.

turkey-vulture.x: type of American vulture, 1823, from turkey + vulture. So called for its bare, reddish head. Distinguished from the black vulture, it was known from 1670s as turkey-buzzard.

turn-spit.x: "dog kept to turn the kitchen roasting-spit by running in a tread-wheel," 1570s; from turn (v.) + spit (n.2).

tween-decks.x: 1816, nautical, shortening of between decks; see tween + deck (n.), with adverbial genitive -s.

type-setter.x: also typesetter, "compositor, one who sets or combines types in order for printing," 1800; see type (n.) in the printing sense + setter.

Toyota.x: Japanese automaker, begun 1930s as a division of Toyoda Automatic Loom Works, named for the family name of the founder. There seems to be no one accepted explanation for the change from -d- to -t-.

Tokyo.x: so named 1868, from Japanese to "east" + kyo "capital;" its earlier name was Edo, literally "estuary."

ted.x: "to spread, turn and spread" (new-mown grass for drying in the air), c. 1300, tedden, from an unrecorded Old English *teddan or from a Scandinavian source akin to Old Norse teðja "to spread manure." It is also related to German verzetteln "to scatter, squander," German dialect zelten "spread out, scatter." Related: Tedding; tedder.

Todd.x: masc. proper name, also a surname (late 12c.), from Middle English todde "fox," a Northern English word of unknown origin. Tod-hole (mid-13c.) was an old provincial word for "fox's den." OED (1989) and Middle English Compendium make no connection of the word to obsolete tod "bush, thick mass of growing foliage"(from Old Norse), despite the old theory [Century Dictionary, 1895] that connects the "fox" word to this on the basis of "bushy tail."

Tommy.x:
"British soldier," 1884, from Thomas Atkins, since 1815 the typical sample name for filling in army forms. Tommy also was, for obscure reasons, a soldier's old colloquial word for "ration bread," hence its use generally and among workers for "food carried to the workplace, provisions," whence it was extended to the company-store system.
Tommy gun (by 1929) is short for Thompson gun (see Thompson). The name was soon extended to other types of sub-machine gun, especially any sort favored by the mob.
Tommy as a pet form of Thomas is by 14c.; other Middle English pet forms (preserved in surnames) include Tomcock, Tomkin, Tomlin.

turner.x: c. 1400, "one whose occupation is to work with a lathe," agent noun from turn (v.) or else from Old French torneor. As a surname from late 13c.

Tex.x: by 1903 as a nickname for a Texan, from a shortening of Texas.

troy.x:
late 14c., troie, standard system of weights for gems and precious metals, from troi weight, weight of Troie, from Troyes, city in France (Roman (Civitas) Tricassium, capital of the Tricasses, a Celtic people whose name was said to mean "those with three tresses").
Troyes was the site of an important fair at which this weight is said to have been used. Large medieval towns had their own standard weights, some of which won broad general acceptance among merchants in other places. The pound troy contains 5,760 grains and is divided into 12 ounces.

Tyler.x: surname, 12c., it means "tile-maker;" see tile (n.) + -er (1). In mid-19c. U.S. political history Tylerism refers to President John Tyler, who was elevated to office by the Whigs but turned renegade to the party once in power.

tsunami.x: "large wave which rolls over and inundates the land," 1896, in reference to the one that struck Japan that year on June 15, from Japanese tsunami, from tsu "harbor" + nami "waves."

til.x: variant of till (prep.) or, properly as 'til, short for until.

Tahoe.x: Lake on the Nevada-California border, from Washo /da'aw/ "lake."

Travis.x: masc. proper name, also a surname (late 12c.), from an Old French word meaning "to cross over," related to traverse (v.). Probably a name for a gatekeeper or the toll collector of a bridge.

Tamil.x: also Tamul, Tamoul, Dravidian people and language of southern India, 1734, from Pali Damila, from Sanskrit Dramila, variant of Dravida (see Dravidian). Related: Tamilian.

Tai.x: group of people of related ethnicity and language in Southeast Asia, including the Thai, Lao, and Shan, from tai, literally "free." Related: Taic.

Tet.x: Vietnamese lunar new year, 1885, short for Tet Nguyen Dan "feast of the first day." The North Vietnamese Tet Offensive in the U.S. Vietnam War began Jan. 30, 1968.

THC.x: active ingredient in marijuana and hashish, 1968, short for tetrahydrocannabinol (1940).

TLC.x: by 1953 as an abbreviation of tender loving care.

TNT.x: also T.N.T., 1915, abbreviation of trinitrotoluene (1908), from trinitro- indicating three nitro- groups in place of three hydrogen atoms in a compound, + toluene.

Tso.x: in Chinese restaurant dishes, a reference to General Tso Tsungtang (1812-1885), military leader during the late Qing dynasty who crushed the Taiping rebels in four provinces. General Tso is considered one of the most famous generals in the history of Hunan province. The chicken dish that bears his name in U.S. Chinese restaurants apparently is modified from a traditional Hunan chung ton gai and may have been named for the general c. 1972 by a chef in New York City during the time Hunan cuisine first became popular among Americans. The dish is named in advertisements for Peng's restaurant in New York City by 1978.

TWA.x: U.S. airline formed May 16, 1928, as Transcontinental Air Transport, merged 1930 with Western Air Express to form Transcontinental and Western Air Inc. (TWA). Name changed to Trans World Airlines 1950, but the abbreviation remained. Its last remnants were bought out by rival American Airlines in April 2001.

Twi.x: chief language of Ghana in West Africa; also known as Akan, by 1874. It is in the Niger-Congo language family.

tad.x: 1877, "young or small child," U.S. colloquial, probably a shortened form of tadpole, which is said to be the source of Tad as the nickname of U.S. President Lincoln's son Thomas (1853–1871). The extended meaning "small amount" is attested by 1915. Tad in other slang references to persons is attested from 1845.

tao.x: 1736, the absolute entity in Taoism, from Chinese tao "way, path, right way (of life), reason." By 1934 as "the way in which life should be ordered" in modern Western conceptions of Confucianism.

tat.x: also tatt, 1882, "to do tatting," a back-formation from tatting or from the same undetermined source. Related: Tatted.

tau.x: nineteenth letter of the Greek alphabet, equivalent to Latin T, early 14c., taw, ultimately from Hebrew taw, last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, literally "sign, mark." In Middle English sometimes taken as a representation of the Cross (or St. Anthony's cross) or the sign of it, also later of the Egyptian ankh (18c.).

tec.x: 1879 in thieves' slang as short for detective (n.); 1934 as short for detective story.

teg.x: sheep in its second year, 1520s, a word of uncertain origin, perhaps from a Scandinavian source (compare Swedish tacka "ewe"). Also formerly applied to a female fallow deer.

tho.x: in modern use, an abbreviated spelling of though. In Old English and Middle English, "those," plural of that (pron.); also as an adverb, "then."

tic.x: condition characterized by twitching of a facial muscle, 1822, often a shortening of tic douloureux "severe facial neuralgia," literally "painful twitch" (1798), from French tic "a twitching disease of horses" (17c.), a word of unknown origin. Klein suggests onomatopoeia; Diez and Century Dictionary compare it to Italian ticchio "whim, caprice, ridiculous habit," itself of unknown origin.

tig.x:
1721, "light touch or tap with the hand," probably from tig (v.) "touch lightly with the hand" (late 15c.) which is of obscure origin, perhaps connected to tick (n.2) "light touch or tap."
As the name of a child's game in which one player chases the others and attempts to touch them, 1816, earlier tick (1620s), perhaps earlier variants of tag (n.2). Tig (n.) "a touch in the game of tag" is by 1821. Tig-tag "to bicker, banter" is from 1640s, said to be a formation from tig.

tix.x: short for tickets, by 1944 in Billboard magazine headlines.

to-.x:
word-forming element of Anglo-Saxon origin expressing separation, division, putting asunder, also "destruction" (on the notion of "apart, asunder," hence "to pieces"). It is reconstructed to be from West Germanic *ti- (source also of Old Frisian ti-, Old High German zi-, German zer-), from Proto-Germanic *tiz-, which is cognate with Latin-derived dis-.
According to OED (1989), some 125 compound verbs with this element are recorded in Old English; Middle English Compendium counts more than 200 verbs and some nouns: In modern spellings to-answer "answer thoroughly;" toswear, tothink, tobeat "beat severely;" tomelt "melt completely;" tocleave "split asunder" (transitive and intransitive); to-squat "flatten, crush," towild "make wild or unruly;" Chaucer writes of a shield to-dashed in combat.
But the number declined rapidly in later Middle English and disappeared by c. 1500 except as conscious archaisms (to-shiver "break to pieces;" all to-brast). In 14c. the to- often appears to be merely emphatic, as if "all too" (to-drunk, to-stink, etc.).

word-forming element of Anglo-Saxon origin, expressing motion, direction, addition; not properly a prefix but the preposition to merged with the following word. This was common in Middle English (to-hear "listen to," to-knit "bind up," to-cast "add together," tocome "arrive, occur, happen;" to-put "affix," to-set, to-stick, to-yield "give up," etc.), but few survive: to-do, together, and time references such as today, tonight, tomorrow — Chaucer also has to-yeere.
Also compare Middle English towhile (conj., adv.) "for as long as; in the meantime." But in toward, to is the principal element, and -ward is the suffix.

tog.x: 1708, "outer garment," since later 18c. usually in plural togs, a shortened from togman "cloak, loose coat" (1560s), a thieves' cant word, formed from French togue "cloak," which is from Latin toga (see toga). Middle English toge "Roman toga" (14c., from Old French and Latin) also was a cant word for "a coat."

tor.x: "high, rocky hill," Old English torr "rock, crag" (said to be a different word from torr "tower"); from a Celtic source cognate with Gaelic torr "lofty hill, mound," Old Welsh twrr "heap, pile;" and perhaps ultimately with Latin turris "high structure" (see tower (n.)). But sources disagree on whether the Celts borrowed it from the Anglo-Saxons or the other way. English tore "projecting ornament" (1550s) also might be related.

tsk.x: sound expressing commiseration or disapproval, 1947; as a verb, tsk-tsk is recorded from 1967. Also as tchick, etc. Related: Tsked.

tun.x:
"large cask," especially one for wine, ale, or beer, Middle English tonne, tunne, from Old English tunne "tun, cask, barrel," a general North Sea Germanic word (compare Old Frisian tunne, Middle Dutch tonne, also Old High German tunna, German tonne). It is also found in Medieval Latin tunna (9c.) and Old French tonne (diminutive tonneau) and perhaps Celtic (compare Middle Irish, Gaelic tunna, Old Irish toun "hide, skin") but all are of uncertain relationship.
As a unit of weight and measure from late 14c., spelled ton and now a separate word (see ton (n.1)).

tup.x: "male sheep," c. 1300, tuppe, perhaps in Old English in place names; it persisted in Scottish and Northern English; a word of unknown origin. As a verb, "to copulate," attested by 1540s. Related: Tupped; tupping.

tut.x: 1520s, along with tush (mid-15c.), an interjection expressing impatient or dismissive contempt.

TGIF.x: also T.G.I.F., by 1946, slang acronym of "Thank God (or goodness), it's Friday" (the day that ended the old work week for most jobs).

Tiki.x: "large wooden image of the creator-ancestor of Maoris and Polynesians," 1777, from Eastern Polynesian tiki "image." Tiki torch as an outdoor party or decorative device was advertised in California newspapers from 1956.

Tina.x: fem. proper name, short for Cristina, etc.

Toby.x:
familiar form of masc. proper name Tobias, in various colloquial usages, such as "drinking mug in the form of a stout old man," usually in 18th-century costume and with a tri-cornered hat (1840). As a type of collar (1882) it refers to that worn by the dog Toby in 19c. Punch and Judy shows. Also in Toby show (by 1942, American English) "comedy act based on the stock character of a boisterous, blundering yokel" (compare rube). It is attested by 1861 in slang as "buttocks."
The thieves' slang noun meaning "highway" (originally with reference to robberies) is by 1807, said to be from Shelta tobar "road."

Tori.x: fem. proper name, originally short for Victoria.

Tupi.x: a native language group of South America, also Tupian, by 1842.

Turk.x:
c. 1300, "person of the dominant race of the Ottoman empire," from French Turc, from Medieval Latin Turcus, from Byzantine Greek Tourkos, Persian Turk, a national name of unknown origin. In Europe traditionally from a mythical son of Japhet. Said to mean "strength" in Turkish. OED (1989) compares Chinese tu-kin, as the ancient name of a people living south of the Altai Mountains (identified by some with the Huns). In Persian, turk, in addition to the national name, also could mean "a beautiful youth," "a barbarian," "a robber," but these are not considered the origin of the name.
In English, the Ottoman sultan was the Grand Turk (late 15c.), and the Turk was used collectively for "the Turkish people" or "Ottoman power" (late 15c.). From 14c. and especially 16c.-18c. Turk was used indiscriminately of Muslim inhabitants of Asia Minor, reflecting the empire's status in the Western mind as the Muslim nation par excellence. Hence Turkery (1580s), Turkism (1590s) for "Islam." To turn Turk was originally "convert to Islam," then generally, "undergo a complete change for the worse" (c. 1600).
 When a man begins to sink in India. and is not sent Home by his friends as soon as may be, he falls very low from a respectable point of view. By the time that he changes his creed, as did McIntosh, he is past redemption. [Kipling, "To Be Filed for Reference," 1899]
Middle English Turkeis (plural), from Old French adjective turcois, also was applied historically to the nomadic tribes of the Middle East in the wars of the Romans and Persians.
The U.S. slang meaning "person of Irish descent" is attested by 1914, apparently originating among Irish-Americans, but the origin is obscure (Irish torc "boar, hog" has been suggested). A Young Turk (1908) was a member of a political group in the Ottoman Empire that sought rejuvenation of the Turkish nation.

thar.x: now representing dialectal pronunciation of there; in literary use in Middle English.

thud.x:
a word more or less imitative and perhaps coined several times in English. Old English had þyddan "to strike, stab, thrust, press." Middle English thudden "push forcefully," also "throw down" (a corpse), c. 1200, is held to be descended from it. The noun is attested from 1510s as "blast of wind;" 1530s as "a loud sound."
The word in the modern senses of "hit with a dull sound; emit a low, blunt sound as by a blow upon a comparatively yielding body," also as the representation of such a sound, is from 1790s. Related: Thudded; thudding.

tiff.x: 1727, "outburst of temper, peevishness," later "petty quarrel, misunderstanding" (1754), of uncertain origin; OED (1989) suggests imitative, "from the sound of a slight puff of air or gas." Related: Tiffy.

tine.x: mid-14c., an alteration of tinde, "horn of an animal, branch of a deer's antlers," also used of the projecting sharp points on a rake, harrow, etc.; from Old English tind "spike, beak, prong, tooth of a fork." This is a general Germanic word (compare Old High German zint "sharp point, spike," Old Norse tindr "tine, point, top, summit," German Zinne "pinnacle") of unknown origin (compare zinc). Related: Tined.

ting.x:
late 15c. as a verb, tingen, "make a light, ringing noise," as a small bell; echoic. Compare tink. Related: Tinged; tinging. As a noun from c. 1600.
Ting-a-ling, a varied reduplication to indicate the sound of a small ringing bell, is by 1879, earlier ting-a-ring (1833). Still earlier such a sound had been represented by ting-tang (1670s); hence also tingle-tangle "disturbance, fuss." originally of the noise of bells (1650s), earlier tinkle-tankle (1610s).

tink.x:
late 14c. tinken (v.), emit a light, short, metallic sound; echoic. By c. 1600 as a noun, "sound made by striking sonant metal with something hard and light" [OED, 1989]. Earlier noun was tinking "act of producing a ringing sound" from a cymbal, etc. (late 14c.).
The verb in the sense of "work as a tinker; mend kettles, pots, etc., by patching them," is from 14c., perhaps a back-formation from tinker (n.), which see, and also compare ting, tinkle.

titi.x: type of small South American monkey, 1832, from native name in Tupi, probably imitative.

toff.x: lower-class London slang for "stylish dresser, man of the smart set," 1851 (Mayhew), said in OED (1989) to be probably an alteration of tuft, formerly an Oxford University term for a nobleman or gentleman-commoner (1755), in reference to the gold ornamental tassel worn on the caps of undergraduates at Oxford and Cambridge whose fathers were peers with votes in the House of Lords. As a verb, "dress up, dress like a toff," by 1915. Related: Toffed; toffing.

tofu.x: soy bean curd, 1876, from Japanese tofu, from Chinese doufu, from dou "beans" + fu "rotten."

togs.x: "clothes," 1779, plural of tog (q.v.) in the canting sense.

toke.x: "inhalation of a marijuana cigarette or pipe smoke," 1968, U.S. slang, from earlier verb meaning "to smoke a marijuana cigarette" (1952), which is perhaps from Spanish tocar in sense of "touch, tap, hit" or "get a share or part." In 19c. the same word in British slang meant "small piece of poor-quality bread," but probably this is not related.

tole.x: "ornamented and painted sheet iron," 1946, from French tôle "sheet iron," from dialectal taule "table," from Latin tabula "a flat board" (see table (n.)).

toon.x: colloquial shortening of cartoon (n.), attested by 1985. It was noted by 1901 as a dialectal pronunciation of tune (n.).

toot.x:
c. 1500, in reference to horns, etc., "give a characteristic sound when blown," ultimately imitative. Compare Middle Low German and Low German tuten "blow a horn."
Transitive sense of "sound (a note, etc.) on a trumpet, horn, etc," is by 1610s; that of "blow" a wind instrument is by 1680s. Related: Tooted; tooting.
Tooting as a strong affirmative (as in you're damned tootin') is attested by 1932, American English (compare 19c. U.S. slang toot (n.) "a blow-out, a spree"). Reduplicated form rootin' tootin' "noisy, rambunctious" is recorded by 1924 and might suggest the sports-fan root (v.2).
1640s, "act of making a tooting noise" (on a horn, etc.), from toot (v.) or independently imitative. By 1790 in U.S. slang as "a blow-out, a spree." The slang meaning "cocaine" is attested by 1977.

tope.x: "to drink heavily," 1650s, a word of unknown origin, perhaps (via French?) from Italian toppa "done!" a word signifying acceptance of a bet. The Romanic word is from a Germanic verb related to tap (v.1); compare Italian toppare "patch," Spanish toper "bump." The notion in betting might be striking hands to seal the bet.

toro.x: "bull," 1650s, from Spanish toro "bull," from Latin taurus (see Taurus). A torista is a bullfight enthusiast who is chiefly interested in the bull.

torr.x: unit of pressure, 1949, named for Italian physicist Evangelista Torricelli (1608-1647), inventor of the barometer.

tosh.x: "neat, clean, trim," 1776, Scottish, of unknown origin. Related: Toshly.
"valuables collected from drains," 1852, London slang, of unknown origin. Related: Tosher.
"nonsense, humbug," 1892, British slang, perhaps a variant of bosh. Related: Toshy.

toss.x:
mid-15c., "to lift or throw upward with a sudden movement;" c. 1500, "have or pitch up and down, or from one place to another," a word of uncertain origin, possibly from a Scandinavian source (compare dialectal Norwegian tossa "to strew, spread").
The transferred sense of "disquiet, agitate" is by 1520s. The food preparation sense (with reference to salad, etc.) is recorded by 1723. The intransitive sense "be restless; throw oneself about" is from 1550s. To toss (s0meone) in a blanket was an old communal expression of dislike. Related: Tossed; tossing.

"an act of throwing, sudden fling or movement." 1630s, from toss (v.). In reference to motions of the head, hair, etc., 1670s. The meaning "a coin toss" is from 1798. In the negative, as something one does not give or care, by 1876. Obsolete alternative noun tossment is from 1640s.
From the "toss of the head" sense came tossy "pertly contemptuous, scornful;" tossily "with affected indifference or carelessness."

toto.x:
"whole, total, all," in various Latin phrases in literary or specialized use; it is the Latin ablative singular (masc. and neuter) of totus "whole, entire" (see total (adj.)).
As toto caelo (with ablative of caelum "the sky") "by the whole heaven, as far apart as the poles," hence "diametrically opposite;" also compare totidem verbis "in so many words," hence "in the very words;" toties quoties "as often as something happens or occasion demands."
English toto- sometimes takes the place of toti-, the regular combining form of Latin totus.

trad.x: 1956, in a Melody Maker headline, a shortening of traditional jazz. Also as a noun, "a traditionalist in jazz." Compare schmaltz. Its general slang use for "traditional" is recorded from 1963.

tram.x:
c. 1500, "beam or shaft of a barrow or sledge," also "a barrow or truck body" (1510s), Scottish, originally in reference to the iron trucks used in coal mines. "The further sense development presents many difficulties, chiefly from the scarcity of early examples" [OED, 1989]. It is probably from Middle Flemish tram "beam, handle of a barrow, bar, rung," a North Sea Germanic word of unknown origin. Century Dictionary compares Norwegian tram "edge, brim," Middle Dutch drom "beam, balk," German tram "a beam."
Many recent senses extended from that "wheeled car or wagon used in coal mines." The sense of "track for a wheeled barrow, continuous line of rails (timber, later iron, etc.) used as a tramway" is by 1826; that of "streetcar" is attested by 1879, short for tram-car "car used on a tramway" (1873).
Middle English also had tramme, used of mechanical devices in astronomy and navigating, also "contrivance" generally, from Old French traime and Anglo-Latin trama, from the same source in the "cart-shaft" sense, so called for appearance.

tref.x: social unit in Wales, Welsh, literally "hamlet, home, town," from PIE *treb- "dwelling" (see tavern).

tres.x: "very," 1819 as a French word in English, from French très, from Old French tres "right, precisely, completely, very," from Latin trans "beyond" (see trans-), later "very" (compare Old Italian trafreddo "very cold").

tri-.x: word-forming element of Latin and Greek origin meaning "three, having three, once every three," from Latin tres (neuter tria) or Greek trias, treis "three" (see three). "The i, etymologically short in Greek and Latin, was in Latin sometimes lengthened, esp. in numerals" [OED, 1989].

trog.x: "obnoxious person, boor, lout," 1956, short for troglodyte (q.v.).

tsar.x: title of the emperor of Russia, 1660s, the more correct Latinization of Russian czar, from prehistoric Slavic *tsesar, via a Germanic source, ultimately from Latin Caesar. Also see czar. Related: Tsardom; tsarevich; tsarina; tsarevna; tsarism.

tuba.x: 1852 in reference to a modern, very large, low-pitched brass musical instrument of the trumpet family, from French tuba, from Latin tuba (plural tubae) "straight bronze war trumpet" (as opposed to the crooked bucina); related to tubus (see tube (n.)).

tufa.x: type of porous rock, 1770, from Italian tufa "tufa, porous rock," probably from Latin tufus, tophus "loose, porous volcanic rock," said to be an Oscan-Umbrian loan-word. Related: Tufaceous.

tuff.x: advertiser's spelling of tough (adj.), attested by 1940.
"light, porous rock," 1560s, from French tufe (16c.), from Italian tufa "porous rock" (see tufa, which is the Italian word taken later directly into English).

tuft.x:
"bunch of soft and flexible things (hairs, feathers, twigs) fixed at the base with the upper ends loose," late 14c., of uncertain origin, perhaps from Old French touffe "tuft of hair" (14c.), which might be from Late Latin tufa "a kind of crest on a helmet" (also found in Late Greek toupha), or from a Germanic source (compare Old High German zopf, Old Norse toppr "tuft, summit;" see top (n.1)).
With excrescent -t following -f-, as in graft (n.1)). As a verb from 1530s. Related: Tufted; tufty.

tuna.x: 1881, from American Spanish (California) tuna, from Spanish atun, from Arabic tun, borrowed, probably in Spain, from Latin thunnus "tunny" (see tunny).

tung.x: 1889, in reference to a type of seed oil obtained from a tree of the same name native to China and Japan, from Chinese tong.

tush.x: "backside, buttocks," 1962, an abbreviation of tochus, tokhus (1914), from Yiddish tokhes, from Hebrew tahat "beneath."
exclamation of impatient rebuke or contemptuous dismissal, mid-15c., tusch; see tut. Related: Tushery.

tutu.x: ballet skirt made up of layers of stiff frills, 1910, from French tutu, alteration of cucu, infantile reduplication of cul "bottom, backside," from Latin culus "bottom, backside, fundament" (from PIE *kuh-lo- "backside, rear;" source also of Old Irish cul "back," Welsh cil "corner, angle"), but the ultimate origin is obscure [de Vaan].

twat.x:
"female pudendum," 1650s, of unknown origin. A general vulgar term of abuse since 1920s.
Robert Fletcher used the word in his 1656 translation of Martial. Bailey's 1730 edition of the "Universal Etymological English Dictionary" has it (defined as pudendum muliebre, as are other slang names for the part), and also has twat-scowerer "a surgeon or doctor."
Robert Browning used it in "Pippa Passes," unaware of its meaning.
 Then owls and bats, 
 Cowls and twats, 
 Monks and nuns, 
 In a cloister's moods. 
Once it was identified, Browning said he found it in a 1660 Royalist rhyme against Sir Henry Vane:
 They'd talk't of his having a Cardinalls Hat, 
 They'd send him as soon an Old Nuns Twat. 
and confessed he hadn't known what it was, but, "The word struck me a distinctive part of a nun's attire that might fitly pair off with the cowl appropriated to a monk."

twee.x: "tiny, dainty, miniature," 1905, from childish pronunciation of sweet (adj.). Compare tummy from stomach.

twi-.x:
word-forming element of Germanic origin meaning "two, twice, double, in two ways;" from Old English twi- "two, in two ways, twice, double," from Proto-Germanic *twi- (source also of Old Frisian twi-, Old Norse tvi-, Dutch twee-, Old High German zwi-, German zwei-). This is reconstructed to be from PIE *dwis (source also of Sanskrit dvi-, Greek di-, Old Latin dvi-, Latin bi-, Lithuanian dvi-), a compounding form from the root *dwo- "two."
Cognate with bi-, it was the regular combining form for "two" in Old English. The few words in it that survived into Middle English include twinter "two years old" (of cattle, sheep, etc.), reduced from Old English twi-wintre, and Old English twispræc "double or deceitful speech," twibill "axe with two cutting edges." Wycliffe (1382) has twisel-tonge "malicious gossip, slanderer," on the notion of "double-tongued." Also compare twilight, a Middle English coinage.

typo.x: 1816, "compositor," short for typographer; 1892 as short for typographical error.

tyre.x: variant spelling of tire (n.), chiefly British English.

Taino.x: an indigenous people of the Caribbean at the time of Columbus, from Taino (Arawakan) nitayno "the first, the good." Also the name of their language. Compare Arawakan.

Tambo.x: "tambourine player in a minstrel troupe," especially as one of the end-men (opposite Bones), by 1844, American English, shortened from tambourine., also the word for the instrument he has.

Taser.x:
1972, formed (probably on model of laser, etc.) from the initials of Tom Swift's electric rifle, a fictitious weapon. A word that threatens to escape the cage of its trademark, despite the strenuous efforts of the owners, who are within their rights to fight to hold it. They also insist, via their attorneys, that it be written all in capitals. Tom Swift was the hero of a series of early 20c. American sci-fi/adventure novels, one of which was titled "Tom Swift and His Electric Rifle."
The noun has spawned a verb, taze or tase. Related: Tased; tasing.

Teton.x: member of a western Sioux people, 1806, from Dakota titonwan, literally "dwellers on the prairie," from thi + huwa. The name is unrelated to the Grand Teton mountain range.

Thoth.x: ancient Egyptian god of wisdom and magic, hieroglyphics, and the reckoning of time, from Latin, from Greek Thoth, from Egyptian Tehuti. Usually represented as a human figure with the head of an ibis. By the Greeks, assimilated to their Hermes.

Thule.x:
region or island at northernmost part of the world, Old English Þyle, from Latin, from Greek Thylē "land six days' sail north of Britain" (Strabo, quoting a lost portion of a work by Polybius, itself based on a lost account of a voyage to the north by 4c. B.C.E. geographer Pytheas of Marsellies).
To the Elizabethans, "the period of cosmography." The identity of the place and the source of the name sparked 2,000 years of speculation; Polybius and Strabo disbelieved the account. Since Roman times the name has been used in a transferred sense of "extreme limits of travel" (Ultima Thule).
 The barbarians showed us where the sun set. For it happened in those places that the night was extremely short, lasting only two or three hours; and the sun sunk under the horizon, after a short interval reappeared at his rising. [Pytheas] 
The name was given to a trading post in Greenland in 1910, site of a U.S. air base in World War II. Related: Thulean. Middle English had it as Tile "northernmost island of the sea," from Old English Tile, a variant (see th).

Tiber.x: river through Rome, considered to be likely from Celtic dubro "river" (compare Dover). Related: Tiburtine., attested from mid-15c. in reference to stone, quarried in the district of Tibur (modern Tivoli) in Latium, also known as tiber-stone.

Tibet.x: country in central Asia, said to be a corruption in Chinese or Arabic of Bod, indigenous name, which is of unknown origin. As an adjective in English, Tibetian is older (1747) but Tibetan (1822) is now the usual word. With combining form Tibeto-.

Tonga.x: from a native name of the African people. Related: Tongan.

Tonto.x: former term for the Western Apaches, from Spanish, literally "foolish;" probably a translation of a name given to the people by other branches of the Apache, such as Chiricahua Apache /bini:'édiné/, Mescalero Apache /bini:'édinendé/, both literally "people without minds," and used to designate the Western Apaches. Spanish tonto is said to be originally a nursery word, used for its sound [Buck], but in some sources it is given as perhaps literally "thunderstruck," from Latin attonius, whence also Spanish atonar "to stupefy" (compare astonish).

Topsy.x:
slave-girl character in Stowe's "Uncle Tom's Cabin" (1852), long a cliche figure for her response to a question put to her by the pious Northern abolitionist Miss Ophelia:
 "Have you ever heard anything about God, Topsy?" 
 The child looked bewildered, but grinned, as usual. 
 "Do you know who made you?" 
 "Nobody as I knows on," said the child, with a short laugh. 
 The idea appeared to amuse her considerably; for her eyes twinkled, and she added-- 
 "I spect I grow'd. Don't think nobody never made me." 
"I spect I grow'd" is often misquoted by the addition of a "just" (or "jes'"); the line sometimes was used inappropriately to indicate something that got large without anyone intending it or noticing.

Torah.x: in reference to Hebrew literature or Jewish custom, "the Pentateuch," hence "Mosaic law" generally, 1570s, from a specific use of Hebrew torah "instruction; law; decision or instruction in a matter of law or conduct given by sacred authority," verbal noun from horah "he taught, showed."

Tudor.x: by 1753 in reference to the English royal family 1485-1603, from Welsh surname Tewdwr, used of the line of English sovereigns from Henry VII to Elizabeth I, descended from Owen Tudor, who married Catherine of France, widowed queen of Henry V. The name is the Welsh form of Theodore. Applied by 1806 to a style of architecture prevalent during these reigns; hence Tudorbethan (1933), Tudory in disparaging reference to excessive use of mock-Tudor.

Turin.x: city in northern Italy, Italian Torino, Roman Augusta Taurinorum, probably from the Taurini, a Ligurian people who had a capital there, the name perhaps from Celtic *tauro "mountain" or *tur "water," but long interpreted by folk etymology as from Latin taurus "bull." Related: Torinese.

Tyrol.x: former crown-land of Austria-Hungary, German Tirol, said to be ultimately from Celtic tir "land" (see Tyrone). Related: Tyrolean.

ta-ta.x: also tata, "good-bye," familiar salutation in parting, 1823, first noted as infant's speech. Abbreviation T.T.F.N., "ta-ta for now," popularized 1941 by BBC radio program "ITMA," where it was the characteristic parting of the Cockney cleaning woman character Mrs. Mopp, voiced by Dorothy Summers.

taffy.x: coarse candy made from sugar or molasses boiled down and cooled, 1817, related to toffee (OED 1989 calls it an earlier form of it), but of uncertain origin; perhaps associated with tafia (1763), name of a rum-like alcoholic liquor distilled from molasses, a word of uncertain origin, perhaps a Creole shortening of ratafia. On this theory, the candy would have been made from the syrup skimmed off the liquor during distillation.

taiga.x: belt of coniferous forests in Siberia, 1869, from Russian taiga, which is of Mongolian origin.

taker.x: "one who takes" in any sense, late 14c., specifically "someone who arrests or captures," agent noun from take (v.). As "one who accepts a bet," by 1810.

talky.x: "loquacious, abounding in talk," 1815, from talk (n.) + -y (2). Related: Talkiness.

talus.x: "anklebone," 1690s, from Latin talus "ankle, anklebone, knucklebone" (plural tali), related to or a derivative of Latin taxillus "a small die, cube" (they originally were made from the knucklebones of animals), which is of obscure origin.

"slope," 1640s, from French talus (16c.), from Old French talu "slope, mound, small hill" (12c.), probably from Gallo-Roman *talutum, from Latin talutium "a slope or outcrop of rock debris," which is perhaps of Celtic origin (compare Welsh, Breton tal "forehead, brow").
OED (1989), however, suggests derivation from root of talus (n.1) in the sense of "heel" which developed in its Romanic descendants. Mainly used of military earthwork at first; the meaning "sloping mass of rocky fragments that has fallen from a cliff" is attested by 1830.

tamer.x: "one who or that which domesticates or brings into subjection," c. 1400, agent noun from tame (v.).

tango.x:
syncopated ballroom dance, 1913 (the year it became a rage in Britain and America), from Argentine Spanish tango, originally the name of an African-South American drum dance, probably from a Niger-Congo language (compare Ibibio tamgu "to dance"). Phrase it takes two to tango was a song title from 1952. As a verb from 1913. Related: Tangoed.
 ON DANCING (NOTE.—Dancing is pronounced two ways,—Tahn-go, or Tan-go. depending on your social status.) [The Gargoyle, University of Michigan, November 1913]
 It is hardly a year ago since the Tango reached this country from South America by way of Paris. It was at first no more than a music-hall freak. But some of those mysterious people who inspire new social fashions were attracted by its sinuous movements and the strange backward kick, and this year it made its way into private houses as well as public ball rooms. [The Living Age, Dec. 13, 1913]
 "I need not describe the various horrors of American and South American negroid origin. I would only ask hostesses to let one know what houses to avoid by indicating in some way on their invitation cards whether the 'turkey-trot,' the 'Boston' (the beginner of the evil), and the 'tango' will be permitted." [quoted in Current Opinion, October 1913, as from a letter to the London Times]
