theandric.x: 1610s, "pertaining to God and man; existing by the union of divine and human natures, part human part divine," from Latinized form of Greek theandrikos "being both god and man;" see theo- "god" + andro- "man."

theatrics.x:
1807, "matters pertaining to the stage, all that pertains to dramatic performance," from noun use of theatric (adj.) "pertaining to the theater" (1706); see theater; also see -ics. The meaning "theatrical behavior" is attested by 1929, American English.
There were earlier uses of theatric as a noun meaning "drama as a craft" (late 15c.). Theatricals (n.) was used from 1650s as "stage plays," from 1763 as "matters pertaining to the stage."

theirself.x: emphatic plural pronoun, c. 1300, from their + self, with self, originally an inflected adjective but here it has come to be treated as a noun meaning "person." Related: Theirselves. Compare themselves.

theomachy.x: 1560s, "a fighting against the gods;" 1858 "a battle among the gods;" the elements are Greek theos "god" (see theo-) + makhē "a battle, fight" (see -machy). Greek theomakhia was "a battle of the gods."

theomania.x:
"form of insanity in which the sufferer imagines himself to be a god," 1814 (by 1810 in German); see theo- "god" + mania "mental derangement." Related: Theomaniac.
 The term Theomania has been applied to the variety [of religious monomania] in which pride and vanity are united to religious hallucinations ; those who are thus afflicted conceive themselves to be God or Christ, or that they have intercourse with spirits and so forth.
 Others conceive that they are possessed of the devil—that they are damned, &c. The term Demonomania has been applied to this variety, in which fear and remorse are prevalent. [Alexander Morison, Cases of Mental Disease, Edinburgh, 1827]

therefrom.x:
"away from there, from that place, thence," mid-13c., ther-from. One word from 17c.; see there + from.
Middle English also had thereforth (late 13c.) "to that place; by that place," also "from hence, away from there," which is obsolete in both senses. Other Middle English words in similar senses included thereaway (early 15c.), therehence (c. 1300).

thereunto.x: "to it, toward it, at it," c. 1300, ther-unto; see there + unto. Compare thereto.

thereupon.x:
late 12c., þer uppon, "on top of that;" see there + upon. From 14c. as "immediately after that;" by 1530s as "in consequence of that."
Thereup (late Old English ther-up) "on it, on top of it" is obsolete.

therewith.x:
c. 1200, ther-with, "along with, in company with;" mid-13c., "by means of that;" from there + with. Old English þær wiþ meant "against; in exchange for," which continued in early Middle English. Similar formation in Swedish dervid, Danish derved.
Middle English also had therewithin "inside that place, within it; into that place" (Old English þær-wiþinnan); therewithout (adv.) "outside that or it; in the absence of that, lacking that" (late 12c.).

thermotic.x: "of or relating to heat," 1874, adjective from Greek thermē "heat, feverish heat" (from PIE root *gwher- "to heat, warm"). Earlier, thermotics was proposed by Whewell as a name for the science which treats of heat (1831), along with photistics for that which treats of light, but they did not last. Related: Thermotical.

thickener.x: 1650s, "that which makes thick or thicker," agent noun from thicken (v.). Later especially of substances used in fabric-dyeing to prevent spreading.

thinkable.x: 1805, "imaginable as fact;" possibly a back-formation from unthinkable. Later "capable of being thought, cogitable" (1854), from think (v.) + -able.

thirtieth.x: "next in order after the twenty-ninth; an ordinal numeral; being one of thirty equal parts into which a whole is regarded as divided;" Middle English thretyth, from Old English þritigoða; see thirty + -th (1). Respelled 16c. to conform to new spelling of thirty. Compare three.

thornless.x: "lacking thorns," as a rosebush, etc., by 1776, from thorn (n.) + -less.

throughly.x: "fully, completely," mid-15c., from through + -ly (2). Hence "without reserve." The archaic alternative form of thoroughly.

throwback.x: also throw-back, "reversion to an ancestral type or character," 1888, from the verbal phrase; see throw (v.) + back (adv.). To throw back "revert to ancestral character" was a breeder's term, attested by 1879. Earlier throw-back (n.) meant "a reverse in a course or progress, a relapse" (1856). The verbal phrase, meaning "reflect" (as of light) is attested from 1831.

thyroxine.x: active principle of the thyroid gland, 1915, from thyro-, combining form of thyroid, + oxy- (apparently a reference to the oxygen atom present in it, but OED has it as a shortening of oxy-indol) + chemical suffix -ine (2), denoting an amino acid.

tick-tock.x:
representing the slow, recurrent ticking of a tall clock, by 1845, a reduplication based on tick (n.2). Other representations of a clock or watch-like sound include tick-tack (1540s), tick-tick (1670s), tick-a-tack (1865).
To tock (v.) "make a sound slightly lower than tick" is by 1913, tocked (of a clock, with ticked).

tightrope.x: also tight-rope, "tensely stretched rope on which an acrobat performs dextrous feats," 1801, from tight (adj.) + rope (n.). So called for being tensely stretched. Compare funambulist. Tight-rope walk (n.) in the figurative sense "dangerous act requiring skill and finesse" is by 1928.

time-line.x: also timeline, 1876, "line following fractions of seconds in measuring," from time (n.) + line (n.). By 1967 "a schedule, a deadline."

timepiece.x: any apparatus or machine by which the progress of time is recorded or measured, also time-piece, 1765, from time (n.) + piece (n.1).

tin-plate.x: "sheet-iron coated in tin," 1670s, from tin (n.) + plate (n.).

tinderbox.x: also tinder-box, "box in which tinder and flint are kept ready for use," 1520s, from tinder + box (n.); figurative or colloquial extension to anything easily inflammable, especially " 'inflammable' person or thing," is attested from 1590s.

tiredness.x: "state of being weary, wearied condition, fatigue," early 15c., glossing Latin fatigacio; from tired + -ness.

titration.x: in chemistry, "volumetric analysis, process for establishing of a standard strength or degree of concentration of a solution or compound," 1864, noun of action from titrate (v.).

tombstone.x:
1560s, "flat stone placed atop a grave" (or the lid of a stone coffin); from tomb + stone (n.). The meaning "gravestone, headstone" is attested from 1711, extended to any memorial marker on a grave including wooden boards cut in the shape of headstones.
The city in Arizona, U.S., is said to have been named by prospectors who in 1877 found silver there after being told they would find only their tombstones (the story is by 1880). A tombstone advertisement (1947) is one which displays a list of names of those associated with a new venture or issue, perhaps so called for its unvarying wording.

toothpick.x: also tooth-pick, "implement (of wood, ivory, etc.) for cleaning teeth of substances stuck between them," late 15c., from tooth (n.) + pick (n.). Old English had toðsticca, and pick-tooth, tooth-picker in the same sense are attested from 1540s. As U.S. slang for "Bowie knife" by 1867.

top-notch.x:
also top notch, "best quality, most stylish," 1840, a vogue phrase c. 1841, from top (adj.) + notch (n.). It is evidently figurative of a "highest point," but the exact mechanical image is uncertain. At the time it was the name of a part in umbrella patents.
 If a young blade drives his vehicle so as to pass others who are in his party, he is said to "tip them the go by."—If his dress consists of articles which are "all the rage," he is "quite the top notch." It is remarkable that these and similar phrases are most in use among people who claim distinction in the fashionable world. [Boston Weekly Magazine, June 12, 1841] 
 Malgre the dislike of others to an extensive cultivation of cranial shrubbery, I consider long hair an honor unto a man, his glory and his charm. The beauty of the willow is its branches. Deprived of these and all its gracefulness has departed. The tassel of some vegetables is the top notch of their loveliness. ["Long Hair" in Rural Repository (Hudson, N.Y.), July 18, 1840]

torchiere.x: also torchere, "large, decorated candelabrum," 1910, from French torchère, from torche (see torch (n.)). The word was used in the French form in English by 1891.

tormentor.x: c. 1300, tormentour, "judicial torturer, official charged with executing cruel punishments," also "anyone who causes physical pain or mental distress;" from Anglo-French tormentour, Old French tormenteor "torturer," agent noun from tormenter "to torture" (see torment (v.)). Related: Tormentress (early 15c., often of Fate).

touchdown.x:
1864, originally in rugby, "act of placing the ball on the ground beyond a goal line with the result of scoring points," from the verbal phrase (attested by 1859 in sports); see touch (v.) + down (adv.). Touch (n.) as "an act of touching the ground with the ball behind the goal" is attested by 1857.
As "landing of an aircraft" by 1935, from the verbal phrase in that sense.

touchwood.x: "soft white or yellowish substance that burns for hours," 1570s, from touch (v.) + wood (n.). It is a product of wood rotted by certain fungi; said to be probably so-called from the notion of being set alight at the "touch" of a spark.

tournedos.x: as tourne-dos, steak dish, 1869, from French, from tourner "to turn" (see turn (v.)) + dos "back" (see dossier). The recipe appeared in French sources in mid-19c. An early text called it "Tournedos, ou, escalopes de boeuf sautées." According to French etymologists, "so called because the dish is traditionally not placed on the table but is passed behind the backs of the guests" [OED, 1989]. But there are other theories. It is the name of a village in Normandy, and was also the name for a type of administrator at fish markets who oversaw the sale of foodstuffs that were less than fresh.

tow-truck.x: truck outfitted with special equipment for freeing stuck vehicles or moving others that want moving, by 1917, from tow (v.) + truck (n.).

towelette.x: "small towel," 1896, originally a trade name, from towel (n.) + -ette.

townhouse.x: also town-house, 1825, "a residence in a town," from town (n.) + house (n.). From a time when well-off families had country houses as well. As a type of suburban attached housing, c. 1968, American English. Earlier it could mean "a town hall, building containing town offices" (1520s).

traceable.x: "capable of being traced," in any sense, 1748, from trace (v.) + -able. Related: Traceability.

trachelo-.x: word-forming element meaning "of the neck, having the form of a neck, of the neck and," from Latinized form of Greek trakhēlos "the neck, throat," which Beekes describes as "Probably a Greek innovation" probably related to a root for "turning" (he compares Old Church Slavonic vratiti "to turn," also Lithuanian kalkas).

trackless.x: "pathless, untrodden, not marked by a track," 1650s, from track (n.) + -less. Attested earlier in erroneous form tractless (1620s), but there likely meaning this.

trade-off.x: also tradeoff, "sacrifice of one benefit for another," 1959, from verbal phrase trade off, which is attested by 1793 in the meaning "dispose of by barter;" see trade (v.) + off (adv.).

tradesman.x: "shopkeeper, person employed in trade," 1590s, from genitive of trade (n.) + man (n.). Tradeswoman is by 1707. Tradesfolk "persons employed in trade" is by 1760.

trainable.x: "capable of being educated or drilled," 1540s, from train (v.) + -able. Related: Trainability.

trampoose.x: "walk or wander about," 1798 (implied in tramboozing), a fanciful elaboration of tramp (v.) used occasionally 19c.

transaxle.x: in a motor vehicle, 1958, from a contraction of transmission axle.

transduce.x: "alter the nature or medium of" a signal, by 1944; a back-formation from transducer. Related: Transduced; transducing.

transeunt.x: "passing outward," variant of transient (adj.), usually in a modern psychological sense of "operating beyond or outside itself" (opposite of immanent).

trap-door.x: "door set flush in a floor or ceiling," often hidden and leading to a passageway or secret place, late 14c., trappe-dore; see trap (n.1) + door (n.). Trap-door spider, in reference to one of several formidable-looking species whose nest is a tube in the soil with a hinged lid like a trap door, is attested by 1835. The tube is for the spider's concealment and safety, not to capture prey.

trapezius.x: large muscle over the back of the neck, by 1704, from Modern Latin trapezius (musculus), masc. adjective from trapezium (see trapezium). So called from the shape they form. Related: Trapezial "of or pertaining to the trapezius" (1660s).

trattoria.x: "Italian restaurant," 1832, from Italian trattoria, from trattore "host, keeper of an eating house," from trattare "to treat," from Latin tractare "manage, handle, deal with, conduct oneself toward," originally "drag about, tug, haul, pull violently," frequentative of trahere (past participle tractus) "to pull, draw" (see tract (n.1)). The Latin word also produced French traiteur, "caterer."

treadmill.x:
appliance for producing rotary motion by weight of a man (or animal) on movable steps connected to a revolving wheel; originally an instrument of prison discipline. It was invented (and named) 1822; see tread (v.) + mill (n.1). 
 As a corrective punishment, the discipline of the stepping mill has had a most salutary effect upon the prisoners, and is not likely to be easily forgotten, while it is an occupation which by no means interferes with, nor is calculated to lessen the value of, those branches of prison regulation which provide for the moral and religious improvement of the criminal. ["Description of the Tread Mill Invented by Mr. William Cubitt of Ipswich for the Employment of Prisoners," London, 1822] 
Figurative of a monotonous or wearisome round by 1827, but by later generations regarded as a path to physical fitness. Treadwheel is attested by 1570s in reference to a similar method of driving machinery, by a man or animal, for purely mechanical or industrial purposes.

tree-ring.x: one of the visibly marked sections of the wood of a tree, in concentric circles, roughly indicating a year of its growth, by 1919, from tree (n.) + ring (n.). Earlier they were called annual rings (by 1906). Cross-identification of ring sequences in different trees was recognized as a way to determine dates by 1911.

triathlon.x: 1970, from tri- "three" + Greek athlon "contest;" formed on model of decathlon, biathlon, etc. Originally of various combinations of events; one of the earliest so called combined clay-pigeon shooting, fly-fishing, and horse-jumping; another was cross-country skiing, target shooting, and a giant slalom run; and a third connected to the U.S. Army involved shooting, swimming, and running. Applied to the combination of a long swim, a bicycle-race, and a marathon by 1981.

tribalism.x: 1868, "condition of being a tribe; state of existing in separate tribes," from tribal + -ism. The meaning "group loyalty" (in modern politics, etc.) is attested by 1955.

tribesman.x: "man belonging to a tribe," 1798, from genitive of tribe (n.) + man (n.).

trickster.x: "one who practices tricks," 1711, from trick (n.) + -ster. Tricker as "one who tricks" is by 1560s.

tricuspid.x: "having three points," 1660s, from Latin tricuspidem (nominative tricuspis) "three-pointed," from tri- (see tri-) + cuspis "point" (see cusp). As a noun, short for tricuspid tooth, by 19c. Related: Tricuspidal; tricuspidate.

triennial.x:
1630s, "continuing three years;" 1640s, "occurring every three years;" with -al (1) + Latin triennium "three-year period," from tri- "three" (see tri-) + annus "year" (see annual (adj.)). For the vowel change, see biennial.
As a noun, "a third anniversary," by 1630s. Middle English triennal was "a mass said for three years for the soul of one dead" (late 14c.), from Medieval Latin triennale. Related: Triennially.

trilobite.x: extinct marine arthropod of the order Trilobita, 1820, from Modern Latin Trilobites (Walch, 1771), from Greek tri- "three" (see three) + lobos "lobe" (see lobe); so called for the three longitudinal lobes into which its body is divided. Related: Trilobitic. Extinct from the close of the Carboniferous, they are among the largest and most widely known fossils in the extensive Cambrian and Silurian beds of England (compare locust).

triumphal.x: early 15c., "celebratory of a victory," military or spiritual, from Old French trionfal, triumphal, or directly from Latin triumphalis, from triumphus (see triumph (n.)). Triumphous "celebrating victory" is from late 15c.; also compare triumphant. Related: Triumphally; triumphalism.

triweekly.x: also tri-weekly, 1832, "occurring, appearing, or performed once every three weeks;" see tri- + weekly. Less correctly, "thrice a week," from 1809, in reference to newspapers.

troublous.x: early 15c., "turbid, murky," also "mentally or emotionally distressed, full of troubles or misfortunes" and "causing trouble or grief" (mid-15c.); from Old French troblos, torblos, troubleus, from truble/torble (see trouble (n.)). Also compare troublesome, troubled. Related: Troublousness "distracting or disturbing behavior, troublemaking." Hoccleve complains of this troubly world. Troublable "easily stirred up" is attested late 14c., from Old French.

trousseau.x: "a bride's clothing, etc., brought from her former home," 1817, from French trousseau, originally "a bundle," diminutive of Old French trousse "bundle" (see truss (n.)). Italicized at first, nativized by 1833. The Old French word was borrowed into Middle English early 13c. as "a bundle of keys," but it fell from use.

trumpeter.x: "one who sounds a trumpet; one who announces or calls attention," late 15c., agent noun from trumpet (v.). Trumpeter-swan, a large North American species, is so called by 1842.

truthless.x: late 12c., treuthles, "lacking faith in God," from truth + -less. From late 14c. as "lacking truthfulness;" c. 1400 as "not real." Related: Truthfully; truthfulness.

tunesmith.x: "composer of popular songs," 1926, U.S. colloquial coinage (jazz slang), from tune (n.) + smith (n.). Sometimes derogatory.

turbulent.x: early 15c., of liquids, "cloudy, impure;" mid-15c., of persons, "disorderly, tumultuous, unruly;" from Old French turbulent (12c.), from Latin turbulentus "full of commotion, restless, disturbed, boisterous, stormy," figuratively "troubled, confused," from turba "turmoil, crowd" (see turbid). In reference to weather, by 1570s. Related: Turbulently.

turnabout.x: also turn-about, "action of doing something alternately or successively," 1640s, from verbal phrase; see turn (v,) + about (adv.).

turnstile.x: also turn-stile, mid-15c., "post surmounted by horizontal arms which move round as a person passes through," from turn (v.) + stile (n.). Used to admit persons and bar horses, cattle, carts, etc., or to bar persons until toll money is collected. A turnpike originally was a form of it.

turntable.x: also turn-table, "circular platform designed to turn upon its center," 1835, from turn (v.) + table (n.). Originally in railway use, a platform with a line of rails across it for turning locomotives at the end of the line. The record-player sense is attested by 1908.

turquoise.x:
opaque greenish-blue precious stone, 1560s, from French, replacing Middle English turkeis, turtogis (late 14c.), from Old French fem. adjective turqueise "Turkish," in pierre turqueise "Turkish stone." So called for being brought to Europe first from Turkestan or via Turkish Ottoman lands.
As an adjective, in reference to color, 1570s; as a color name, attested from 1853 (turquoise-blue is from 1799). Cognate with Spanish turquesa, Medieval Latin (lapis) turchesius, Middle Dutch turcoys, German türkis, Swedish turkos, etc. "Chemically it is a hydrated phosphate of aluminum and copper" [Flood].

twentieth.x:
"next in order after the nineteenth; an ordinal numeral; being one of twenty equal parts into which a whole is regarded as divided;" 16c., from twenty + -th (1).
It replaced Middle English twentithe, from Old English twentigoða. Middle English also had as a numeral twentiand, with substitution of Old Norse suffix. The Twentieth Century Limited was an express train from New York to Chicago 1902-1967.

twi-night.x: 1939, in reference to evening double-header baseball games, from twilight + night.

twist-off.x: of bottle or jar caps, 1959, from the verbal phrase; see twist (v.) + off (adv.).

two-faced.x: "deceitful, double-dealing," 1610s; see two + face (n.); two faces or tongues was an ancient image of duplicity. In early use also twi-faced (1630s). As "having two faces" (as the Roman Janus), by 1650s.

tympanist.x: 1610s, "one who plays on a drum," from Latin tympanista, from Greek tympanistēs, from tympanizein, from tympanon (see tympanum). Since mid-19c. specifically of players on kettledrums.

Theodosian.x: "of or pertaining to Theodosius," especially in reference to Roman emperor Theodosius II (408-450). The name is etymologically "gift of the gods," from theos "god" (see theo-) + dosis "a giving," from stem of didonai "to give" (from PIE root *do- "to give").

Tyrrhenian.x: 1650s, "pertaining to the Etruscans," from Latin Tyrrheni, from Greek Tyrrenoi "Tyrrhenians," from tyrsis "tower, walled city" (cognate with Latin turris "tower"). Earlier Tirene (late 14c.).

tablecloth.x: also table-cloth, "cloth for covering the top of a table," mid-15c., from table (n.) + cloth.

tabulation.x: "act or process of making tabular arrangements," 1803, noun of action from tabulate (v.). Latin tabulationem meant "a flooring over." Tabularization (1853) seems to be mostly a dictionary word.

tachymeter.x:
surveying instrument for rapidly locating position, 1836, from tachy- "swift" + -meter. Related: Tachymetry.
 M. GAETANO CAÏRO has invented an instrument, to which he has given the name of 
 Tachymeter ( 
 rapid measurer). Its object is to give the area of plane surfaces bounded by any outline whatever, without the necessity of any arithmetical operation. [Magazine of Popular Science and Journal of the Useful Arts, vol. ii, 1836]

talebearer.x: also tale-bearer, "tattle-tale," late 15c., from tale (n.) + agent noun from bear (v.).

talking-to.x: "a reprimand," 1871, from euphemistic use of verbal phrase talk to "address stern words to, rebuke," which is attested by 1860 (see talk (v.)).

tarantella.x:
1782, "peasant dance popular in Italy," a rapid, whirling dance for one couple; earlier "hysterical malady characterized by an extreme impulse to dance" (1630s). It was epidemic 15c.-17c. in Apulia and adjacent parts of southern Italy and was popularly attributed to (or believed to be a cure for) the bite of the tarantula.
This is likely folk-etymology, however, and the names of the dance and the spider more probably share an origin in Taranto, the name of a city in southern Italy (see tarantula). The word was used in English by 1833 for the style of music that accompanies the peasant dance; it is usually in 6/8 time with whirling triplets and abrupt major-minor modulations. Related: Tarantism. The dance-bitten are tarantati (fem. tarantate).
 Those who were bitten generally fell into a state of melancholy, and appeared to be stupified, and scarcely in possession of their senses. This condition was, in many cases, united with so great a sensibility to music, that at the very first tones of their favourite melodies, they sprang up, shouting for joy, and danced on without intermission, until they sank to the ground exhausted and almost lifeless. [Babington's translation of J.F.C. Hecker, "The Epidemics of the Middle Ages," London, 1859]

tattersall.x: fabric with a small and even check pattern, 1891, so called because it was similar to the traditional design of horse blankets, in reference to Tattersall's, the famous London horse market and gambler's rendezvous, founded 1766 by Richard Tattersall (1724-1795). The surname is from the place in Lincolnshire, which is said to represent "Tathere's nook," "probably in the sense 'nook of dry ground in marsh'." [Cambridge Dictionary of English Place-Names]

tattletale.x: also tattle-tale, "one habitually fond of telling tales or spilling secrets," 1880, from tattle (v.) + tale (n.). Probably patterned on telltale (1540s). A 16c. word for "tattle-tale" was pickthank.

tea-kettle.x: also teakettle, "portable kettle with a spout and handle in which to boil water, especially for making tea," 1705, from tea (n.) + kettle (n.).

technetium.x: radioactive metallic element, 1947, coined in Modern Latin from Latinized form of Greek tekhnetos "artificial," from tekhnē "art, skill, craft" (see techno-) + metallic element ending -ium.

technonomy.x: "laws or principles of technology," 1881; see techno- + -nomy.

telegraphy.x: "art or skill of communicating by telegraphy," 1795, from telegraph + -y (1).

telepathic.x: "of or pertaining to telepathy," 1884, from telepathy + -ic. Related: Telepathically.

telephonic.x: 1830, "pertaining to communication by sound over great distances," originally theoretical, from tele- + phonic. From 1834 in reference to the system of Sudré using musical sounds (see telephone), and from 1876 with reference to Bell's electrical invention. In these cases it can be taken as from telephone + -ic. Related: Telephonically.

temperance.x:
mid-14c., temperaunce, "self-restraint, forbearance, moderation" (also a cardinal virtue), from Anglo-French temperaunce (mid-13c.), from Latin temperantia "moderation, sobriety, discretion, self-control," from temperans, present participle of temperare "to moderate" (see temper (v.)).
By late 14c. as "mildness, gentleness," also "observance of a balanced or moderated course of action" generally. Latin temperantia was used by Cicero to translate Greek sōphrosynē "moderation." In English, temperance was used to render Latin continentia or abstinentia, and by mid-16c. the English word was specifically used of moderation or restraint in drinking alcohol and eating; the narrower focus on "total abstinence from intoxicants" is from early 19c., when it arose as a social movement (compare teetotal). Related: Temperancy; temperant.

temporizer.x: "one who complies with prevailing opinion or fashion, a trimmer," agent noun related to temporize (q.v.). For sense, compare time-server.

ten-strike.x: in bowling, a roll of the ball which knocks down all ten pins, by 1840, from ten + strike (n.) in the bowling sense. Hence, figuratively, "something entirely successful or decisive."

tendential.x:
"of the nature of or having a tendency," 1877, from Latin stem of tendency + -al (1). Related: Tendentially.
 Tendenziöse is a term that has become very common in Germany to describe the Tübingen criticism, and has arisen from the lengths to which theologians of this school have shown themselves ready to go, to establish the hypothesis that the New Testament writings arose out of conflicting tendencies in the early church and efforts to bring about compromises between these factions. The word has been transferred in the translation under the form "tendential." [translator's preface to "Hermeneutics of the New Testament" by Dr. Abraham Immer, translated by Albert H. Newman, 1877]

tenderfoot.x:
by 1866, American English, originally a slighting or dismissive term used of newcomers to a Western ranching or mining district, from tender (adj.) + foot (n.). The U.S. equivalent of what in Great Britain was generally called a greenhand. As a level in Boy Scouting, it is recorded from 1908.
 [M]iners illustrate their conversation by the various terms used in mining. I have always noticed how clearly these terms conveyed the idea sought. Awkwardness in comprehending this dialect easily reveals that the hearer bears the disgrace of being a "pilgrim," or a "tender-foot," as they style the new emigrant. ["A Year in Montana," Atlantic Monthly, August 1866] 
Tender-footed (adj.) "cautious", originally of horses, is recorded from 1680s; in reference to persons by 1854.

tenderizer.x: "one who or that which makes tender," in any sense, 1942, agent noun from tenderize. From a culinary preparation to soften meats to a steak-hammer.

tenderness.x: early 14c., tendernesse, "delicacy, sensitivity to pain;" also "capacity for emotion, kindness, compassion;" late 14c. as "youth, immaturity;" from tender (adj.) + -ness.

tendinitis.x: "inflammation of a tendon," 1900, from Medieval Latin tendinis, genitive of tendo (see tendon) + -itis "inflammation."

tenterhook.x:
also tenter-hook, late 15c., "hook for holding or stretching cloth on a tenter," from tenter (q.v.) + hook (n.).
Extended figuratively to anything that painfully strains or tortures; to be on the tenter, on tenters was "on the rack" 1530s, hence "in distress or suspense." The common figurative phrase on tenterhooks "in painful suspense" is attested from 1748; earlier be on tenters (1530s).

teratogeny.x: in pathology, "the production of monsters," 1855, from terato- + -geny. Related: Teratogenesis "production of misshapen organisms," by 1887; in German by 1871.

teratology.x:
1842, "the study of marvels and monstrosities" as a department of biology concerned with malformations, abnormal growths, etc., from terato- + -logy.
Earlier (1670s) it meant "a marvelous narrative, narration of what is prodigious," in that use ultimately from Greek teratologia "a telling of marvels." Related: Teratological; teratologist.

terminable.x:
early 15c., "resolvable, capable of final disposition," with -able + obsolete termine "render a judgment, decide authoritatively" (early 14c.), from Old French terminier and directly from Latin terminare "to mark the end or boundary," from terminus "end, limit" (see terminus).
As "that may come to an end, not perpetual, limitable" by 1580s, from stem of Latin terminare + -able.

terminator.x:
1734, in astronomy, "the line of separation between the bright and dark parts of a moon or planet," from Latin terminator, literally "he who limits or sets bounds," agent noun from terminare "to mark the end or boundary," from terminus "end, limit" (see terminus). The meaning "one who terminates" (something, in any sense) is attested from 1844.
Earlier was terminour "inflectional ending of a word" (c. 1400), from a variant of Old French termineor. Also compare terminate.

testaceous.x: 1640s, "having a hard shell;" 1660s, "of or pertaining to shells," from Latin testaceus "consisting of tiles or shards," from Latin testa "piece of earthenware, tile, potsherd" (see tete).

testicular.x:
"of or pertaining to a testicle or testicles," 1650s, from Latin testiculus (see testicle) + -ar.
Testiculate (adj.), 1760, is "of round or ovoid shape, formed like a testicle," from Late Latin testiculatus "shaped like a testicle; having testicles." Related: Testiculated (1725).

tetrastich.x: "quatrain," 1570s, from Latin tetrastichon, from Greek tetrastikhos, from tetra- "four" (see tetra-) + stikhos "row, line of verse," from PIE *stigho-, suffixed form of root *steigh- "to stride, step, rise" (see stair). Related: Tetrastichic.

theocratic.x: "of, pertaining to, or of the nature of theocracy," 1741; derived probably from theocracy; also see -ic. Related: Theocratical; theocratically.

theodolite.x: type of portable surveying instrument, 1570s, a word of unknown origin and much speculation almost from its first appearance. The inventor seems to have left no account of the coinage. "The word has a Gr[eek] semblance, but no obvious Gr[eek] basis" [Century Dictionary]. Related: Theodolitic.

theophobia.x: "dread or anxious fear of God," by 1807; see theo- + phobia. Latin phrase theophobia Gallicia is by 1800 in English in reference to the atheism of the French philosophes and scientists.

theotechny.x: in classical theater, the appearance of a god on stage in drama or epic; divine intervention, by 1858 (in W.E. Gladstone); the elements are Greek theos "god" (see theo-) + tekhnē "art" (see techno-). Related: Theotechnal (1650s); theotechnic.

thermostat.x: "automatic instrument for regulating temperature," 1831, from thermo- "temperature, heat" + -stat "device for stabilizing or regulating." Related: Thermostatic; thermostatical.

thimblerig.x: con game played with three thimbles and a pea or button, 1825 by this name, though references to thimble cheats, probably the same swindle, date to 1716. Also see rig (v.). Related: Thimblerigger; thumblerigging.

thirteenth.x:
"next in order after the twelfth; an ordinal numeral; being one of twelve equal parts into which a whole is regarded as divided;" a 15c. metathesis of thritenthe, from Old English þriteenþe (see thirteen + -th (1)).
This replaced forms from Old English þreoteoða (West Saxon), þriteogeða (Anglian). Similar formation in Old Norse þrettande, Danish trettende, Swedish trettonde, Old Frisian threttinde, Dutch dertiende, Old High German dritto-zehanto, German dreizehnte. Related: Thirteenthly.

thousandth.x: "last in order of a series of 1,000; one of 1,000 equal parts," 1550s, from thousand + -th (1). Not attested in Old English or Middle English.

thrombosis.x: "coagulation of blood during life, in a blood vessel or the heart," 1706, Modern Latin; see thrombo- + -osis. Greek thrombōsis was "a clumping or curdling," from thrombousthai "become curdled or clotted," from thrombos "clot, curd, lump." Related: Thrombotic.

throughput.x: "energy, activity," 1808 (Jamieson), Scottish; from through + put. Industrial sense is from 1915.

throughway.x: "expressway, large toll road," 1934, American English, from through + way (n.). Middle English had thurgh-weies (plural) "passable ways, passageways" (late 14c.).

thumbscrew.x: also thumb-screw, 1771 "non-lethal instrument of torture that compresses the thumb or thumbs," from thumb (n.) + screw (n.). The thing itself is attested earlier in Scottish as thumbikins (1684, described as a new invention). As "mechanical screw with a broad flat head turned easily by the finger and thumb," by 1794. Related: Thumbscrews; thumb-screws.

thunderous.x: "thunder-producing; loud and deep-sounding," 1580s, from thunder (n.) + -ous. Related: Thunderously.

timberline.x: "elevation at which timber ceases to grow," 1867, from timber (n.) + line (n.). It varies by climate.

time-stamp.x: 1888, "mechanical device for stamping letters, etc., with the date of receipt," from time (n.) + stamp (n.). As a verb by 1906. Related: Time-stamped.

time-table.x: also timetable, "tabular statement showing times for certain activities or events," 1838, originally of railway line arrivals and departures, from time (n.) + table (n.).

tinctorial.x: "pertaining or relating to dyeing or color," 1650s, from French tinctorial, from Latin tinctorius, from tinctor "a dyer," from tingere (past participle tinctus) "to dye" (see tincture).

toiletries.x: "odds and ends used in grooming," 1924, from toiletry "preparation for use in washing or grooming" (1892); see toilet in the older sense of "dressing, grooming" + -ry.

tomfoolery.x: "foolish trifling," 1812, from tom-fool + -ery. In rhyming slang, "jewelry" (1931).

tongueless.x: late 14c., tongeles, "aglossal, having no physical tongue;" early 15c. as "speechless, silent, voiceless," from tongue (n.) + -less. Related: Tonguelessly; tonguelessness.

toothbrush.x:
also tooth-brush, "small brush used for cleaning the teeth," 1650s, from tooth (n.) + brush (n.1). In reference to a type of mustache by 1892.
 It is a remarkable fact that, of eighty-nine men now sitting in the United States senate only nine have beardless faces. ... All the remainder have hirsute growth upon their countenances, ranging in bulk from the toothbrush mustache of Senator Call, of Florida, to the "bearded lady" style affected by Mr. Peffer. ["Hair on the Face," by Walter Wellman, amply illustrated and widely reprinted in U.S. newspapers Jan.-Feb. 1892]

toothpaste.x: also tooth-paste, "paste used for cleaning the teeth," 1832, from tooth (n.) + paste (n.). Earlier substances were tooth-powder (1540s); tooth-soap (c. 1600).

top-hamper.x: nautical, "any unnecessary weight aloft or about the upper decks," 1791, originally the upper masts, sails, and rigging of a sailing ship, from top (n.1) + hamper (n.) in the nautical sense of "things necessary but often in the way."

torpescent.x: "becoming benumbed," 1750, from Latin torpescentem (nominative torpescens), present participle of torpescere "grow stiff or numb, become dull or useless," inchoative of torpere "be numb or stiff" (see torpid). Related: Torpescence "state of being benumbed, state of being incapable of activity or sensibility" (1784).

torrential.x: "pertaining to or resembling a torrent," 1849; see torrent (n.) + -ial. Perhaps by influence of French torrentiel, Spanish torrencial, or English tangential. Related: Torrentially. Blount (17c.) has torrentine as an adjective; Thackeray in 19c. uses torrentuous.

tortellini.x:
in cookery, an Italian (Bolognese) dish consisting of small filled pastas, rolled into rings, 1836, from Italian, plural of tortellino, diminutive of tortello "cake, fritter," itself a diminutive of torta (see torte).
Compare Middle English tourtelet, a type of small dumpling or round cake, from Old French tortelet, a diminutive ultimately from the same source.

tortuosity.x: early 15c., tortuosite, in medical use, "something twisted," from Old French tortuosite, from tortuos (see tortuous), and compare Medieval Latin tortuositas.

touch-hole.x: "small tubular opening through the barrel of a gun or firearm, by means of which the fire is communicated to the charge," c. 1500, from touch + hole (n.). Hence also, from flint-and-steel technology, touch-pan, touch-paper, touch-string.

touchpoint.x: also touch-point, in geometry, "point of contact," c. 1600, from touch + point (n.).

tourmaline.x: brittle crystalline mineral, complete silicate of aluminum and boron, originally obtained from Ceylon, 1759, from French or German, said to be ultimately from Sinhalese toramalli, a general name for cornelian. OED (1989) writes that "the original of the European final -n(e is obscure," and compares mandarin.

tourniquet.x: "instrument for arresting the passage of blood through an artery by compression," 1690s, from French tourniquet "surgical tourniquet," also "turnstile" (16c.), diminutive of torner "to turn," from Old French torner (see turn (v.)). The earliest types consisted of a bandage, a pad, and a screw.

toxicology.x: "branch of medicine treating of poisons and their antidotes," 1815, from French toxicologie (1812), from Latinized form of Greek toxikon "arrow poison" (see toxic) + -logia (see -logy). Related: Toxicological; toxicologically; toxicologist.

tractation.x:
"treatment or handling of a subject, discussion, a discourse or writing," 1550s, from Latin tractationem (nominative tracatio) "a handling, management, treatment; conduct, behavior," also in rhetoric, "discussion," noun from past-participle stem of tractare "handle, manage" (see treat (v.)).
A Roman tractator (fem. tractatrix) was a slave who gave a master massages and oiled the skin, but in post-classical use it also was a "treater" of literary topics or matters.

traitorous.x:
late 14c., traitourous, "guilty of treason, disloyal to a country or sovereign," apparently from Old French traitros "treacherous" (13c.), from traitor (see traitor). Later in a general sense of "treacherous, perfidious, faithless." Related: Traitorously; traitorousness.
Middle English also had traitorly, traitorful, and an alternative form tratious, hence tratiously.

transferee.x: 1736, "one to whom a transfer is made;" 1890s as "one who is transferred;" from transfer (v.) + -ee.

transferor.x: "one who or that which transfers," 1875, legalese agent noun in Latin form, variant of transferer, transferrer (1753), from transfer (v.).

transhuman.x: also trans-human, "beyond human, superhuman," 1812, in a translation of Dante, for his trasumanar, a word he apparently coined; see trans- + human (adj.).

travertine.x: type of soft, porous light-colored rock quarried for building stone, 1797, from Italian travertino, from Latin tiburtinus, from Tiburs, adjective from Tibur (modern Tivoli), in Latium.

treasonous.x: "abounding in or characterized by treason," early 15c. (implied in treasonously), from treason + -ous. Earlier was treasonful (early 14c., treisounful); treasonish "somewhat treasonous" is attested from 1670s.

triangular.x:
c. 1400, "three-sided, triangular in shape," from Late Latin triangularis "triangular; pertaining to a triangle," from Latin triangulus "with three corners" (the usual adjective in classical Latin), as a noun, "a triangle;" see triangle. As "of or pertaining to a triangle" by 1701. The figurative sense of "taking place between three persons or parties" is by 1812. Related: Triangularly.
Triangle (adj.) "three-cornered" is from late 14c. Triangulate (adj.) is attested from early 15c. as "arranged in the shape of a triangle" (from Medieval Latin triangulatus), c. 1600 as "made or composed of triangles." Triangled is late 15c. as "triangular," 1610s as "arranged in triangles." Trianglewise is by mid-15c.
 In the huts of witches all the instruments and implements are triangular. [" 
 Handwörterbuch des deutschen Aberglaubens"]

tricennial.x: "noting 30, occurring once in 30 years," 1650s, from Late Latin tercennium "a space of 30 years." irregularly formed from tricent "thirty each, 30 at a time" (see tri- + cent) + annus "year" (see annual (adj.)). OED cites Blount, Bailey, Webster; perhaps a dictionary word. Related: Tricennarious.

trifarious.x: "of three faces, facing three ways," 1650s, from Latin trifarius; see tri- "three" + -farious.

trigeminal.x: "triple, threefold," originally in anatomy, 1815, with -al (1) + Latin trigeminus "born in threes," as a noun, "triplets;" from tri- (see tri-) + geminus "born at the same birth" (see geminate (adj.)). By 1830 in reference to cranial nerves divided in three branches. Blount (1656) has trigeminous for "being one of three born together."

triliteral.x: "consisting of three letters," 1751, from tri- "three" + Latin littera/litera "alphabetic letter" (see letter (n.1)). Of Semitic languages, in reference to the roots, which in general consist of three consonants each, and which represent the essential idea in the word. Related: Triliteralism.

trillionth.x: "being last in a series of one trillion; one of a trillion parts;" 1820, from trillion + -th (1).

triviality.x: 1590s, "quality of being trivial, paltry character," from French trivialite or else from trivial + -ity. The meaning "a trivial thing or affair" is from 1610s. Related: Trivialities.

trivialize.x: "render trivial, paltry, or commonplace," 1836, from trivial + -ize. Related: Trivialized; trivializing; trivialization.

true-false.x: as a type of test question with only those answers, by 1923; see true (adj.) + false (adj.).

truthiness.x:
"act or quality of preferring concepts or facts one wishes to be true, rather than those known to be true," a catch word popularized in this sense by U.S. comedian Stephen Colbert (b. 1964), declared by American Dialect Society to be "2005 Word of the Year."
It was used in 1832 in a sense of "habit of telling the truth," from truthy "truthful; characterized by truth, resembling truth" (1800), from truth (n.) + -y (2) "full of." Truthlike "like or resembling truth, likely to be true" is attested from 1560s (Drant), and Sidney ("Arcadia," 1586) has truthlikeness for "verisimilitude."

tug-of-war.x:
1670s, "the decisive contest, the real struggle," from tug (n.) in the figurative sense of "supreme effort, strenuous contest of forces" (1650s). As the name of an actual athletics contest of pulling rope, it is attested by 1876.
 When Greek meets Greek then comes the tug of war: when one strong champion meets another of equal prowess the fight is a keen one. [Dixon, "Dictionary of Idiomatic English Phrases," 1891] 
The phrase seems to be modified from a line in Nathaniel Lee's 18c. historical drama about Alexander the Great:
 Clytus. Your father Philip,—I have seen him march, 
 And fought beneath his dreadful banner, where 
 The stoutest at the table wou'd ha' trembl'd. 
 Nay, frown not, sir, you cannot look me dead ; 
 When Greeks joined Greeks, then was the tug of war, 
 The labour'd battle sweat, and conqueft bled. 
 [Nathaniel Lee, "The Rival Queens," 1774]  
 There are twenty Greeks in Chicago, hence when they meet there are ten tugs of war. The Secretary of the Navy should buy up those tugs of war without delay, and then we would have a navy. ["Texas Siftings," Feb. 1883]

tumbleweed.x: also tumble-weed, 1881, detached top of a globular weed that rolls with the wind over U.S. plains in autumn, from tumble (v.) + weed (n.).

tumultuous.x: 1540s, "noisy and disorderly, full of confusion," from French tumultuous (Modern French tumultueux), from Latin tumultuosus "full of bustle or confusion, disorderly, turbulent," from tumultus (see tumult). Related: Tumultuously; tumultuousness. Tumultuary (adj.) "hurriedly done, irregular, done without order or system" is by 1580s.

turnbuckle.x: also turn-buckle, 1703, "catch or fastening for windows and shutters," from turn (v.) + buckle (n.). Meaning "coupling with internal screw threads for connecting metal rods" is attested from 1877.

turtleneck.x:
also turtle-neck, a type of collar (originally of sweaters), 1893, from turtle (n.1) + neck (n.).
What is now termed a "turtleneck" was the regular collar style for sweaters at the time; the appellation appears to have originally been for designating a particular kind of two-layered collar, somewhat like a sailor collar put atop the inner standing neck. Perhaps the name was suggested by the outer "shell" of the second collar. When high collars fell out of fashion c. 1910 the name became applied instead to all high-collar sweaters.
Mock-turtle neck, a high neck style that is sewn into place on a shirt instead of folded over, is by 1957.

two-handed.x: early 15c., "requiring two hands to use or manage;" see two + hand (n.). By 1650s as "adapted for use or performance by two persons;" by 1847 as "having two hands."

typewriter.x:
"machine for mechanical writing printing by the impress of types arranged to strike one at a time onto a moving sheet," by 1868 in patent applications, from type (n.) + writer.
 It is the advantage of the typewriter that, due to its rigidity and its space precisions, it can, for a poet, indicate exactly the breath, the pauses, the suspensions even of syllables, the juxtapositions even of parts of phrases, which he intends. For the first time the poet has the stave and the bar a musician has had. For the first time he can, without the convention of rime and meter, record the listening he has done to his own speech and by that one act indicate how he would want any reader, silently or otherwise, to voice his work. [Charles Olson, "Projective Verse," 1950] 
Among the old slang names for it was office-piano (by 1942).

typography.x: "art of composing types and printing from them," 1640s, from French typographie, from Medieval Latin typographia, from Greek typos (see type (n.)) + -grapheia "writing," from graphein "to write" (see -graphy). It is attested by 1690s as "action or process of printing from types."

Tallahassee.x: place in Florida, U.S.A., 1799, originally Seminole Tallahassee, from Muskogee /talaha:ssi/, name of a tribal town, perhaps from /(i)talwa/ "tribal town" + /ahassi/ "old, rancid" [Bright].

Ticonderoga.x: place in New York state, from Mohawk (Iroquoian) tekotaro:ke "branching (or confluence) of waters," with -otar- "large river, lake."

taciturnity.x: mid-15c., taciturnite, "disinclination to talk, failure to speak," from Old French taciturnité and directly from Latin taciturnitatem (nominative taciturnitas) "a being or keeping silent," from taciturnus "disposed to be silent," from tacitus "silent" (see tacit).

tagliatelle.x: 1876, from Italian tagliatelle, plural noun from tagliare "to cut" (see entail).

tailor-made.x:
by 1830 in the figurative sense of "made or shaped to suit" a person or situation, usually slighting.
 If we can in any way persuade the young ladies, that the highest trait of beauty they can possess, is a countenance of independence and sufficiency to themselves; ... smirking dandies, shop window loiterers, little puny, tailor-made, essenced time killers, will disappear as insects in summer are drowned in honey. [Greenfield, Mass., Gazette, May 11, 1830] 
Perhaps on the contemporary notion of a tailor as "one who makes outer garments to order," as opposed to a clothier, who makes them for sale ready-made. But the expression may owe something to Shakespeare:
 Kent. ... You cowardly rascal, nature disclaims in thee; a tailor made thee. 
 Corn. Thou art a strange fellow: a tailor make a man? 
 Kent. Ay, a tailor, sir: a stone cutter, or a painter, could not have made him so ill, though they had been but two hours at the trade. 
 ["King Lear"] 
The later literal sense (by 1873) was "heavy and plain, with attention to exact fit and with little ornamentation," as of women's garments made by a tailor rather than a dress-maker.

teachership.x: "office, function, or position of a teacher," 1846, from teacher (n.) + -ship.

technicolor.x: "vivid color," 1946, earlier as a trademark name (Technicolor, registered in U.S. 1917) for a process of making color movies, from technical + color (n.). As an adjective from 1940.

technocracy.x:
"control of society or the economy by technical experts," 1919, coined by W.H. Smyth as a name for a new system of government by technical experts, from techno- + -cracy.
 William Henry Smyth, a distinguished engineer of Berkeley, California, wrote at the close of the war a series of thoughtful papers for the New York magazine "Industrial Management", on the subject of "Technocracy". His thesis was the need of a Supreme National Council of Scientists to advise us how best to live, and how most efficiently to realize our individual aspirations and our national purpose. [The Bookman, March 1922]
 In his Introductory address, Dr. Burchard, the Dean of Humanities, spoke with awe of “an approaching scientific ability to control men’s thoughts with precision.” I shall be very content if my task in this world is done before that happens. [Winston Churchill, convocation address, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, March 31, 1949]
There is an earlier use from 1895 in reference to the medical profession.

technophile.x: "technology enthusiast; one who favors technology," 1968, from techno- + -phile.

technophobe.x:
"person who fears technology," by 1952, perhaps by 1946, from techno- + -phobe. Related: Technophobia; technophobic.
 If the reader will consult such a book as 
 Recent Economic Changes, by David A. Wells, published in 1889, he will find passages that, except for the dates and absolute amounts involved, might have been written by our technophobes (if I may coin a needed word) of today. [Henry Hazlitt, "Economics in One Lesson," 1952 edition]

telecommute.x: "work an office job from home by means of phone connections, data links, etc.," by 1974 (as a hypothetical experience), from tele- + commute (v.). Related: Telecommuted; telecommuter (by 1975). Compare telecommuting.

telegraphic.x: "of or pertaining to a telegraph; communicated by telegraph," 1794, originally of semaphore, etc.; from telegraph (n.) + -ic. The electric telegraph sense is by 1823. Related: Telegraphically.

temporality.x: late 14c., "temporal power," a sense now obsolete, from Late Latin temporalitas, from temporalis "of a time, but for a time" (see temporal (adj.1)). The meaning "relation to time, state of being in time" is from 1630s. Temporalty is attested from late 14c. as "worldly goods or concerns," from Old French temporalte.

temporicide.x: 1851, "the killing of time," from stem of Latin tempus "time" (see temporal (adj.1)) + -cide. By 1876 as "one who kills time."

teonanacatl.x: native name for a hallucinogenic fungi (Psilocybe mexicana) found in Central America, 1875, from Nahuatl (Aztecan), from teotl "god" + nancatl "mushroom."

territorial.x:
1620s, "of or pertaining to a land or territory," from Late Latin territorialis, from territorium (see territory). As "of or pertaining to a U.S. territory" by 1791. In reference to British regiments, by 1881; territorial army "British home defense" is by 1907.
In reference to an area defended by an animal, from 1920. Territorial waters is from 1841. Territorial imperative "animal need to claim and defend territory" is attested 1966.
Related: Territorialism, used or suggested in various governance senses by 1865; in zoology, in reference to animal territoriality, by 1933. Territorialize is by 1818 as "extend by addition of territory," later also "reduce to the state or status of a territory" (by 1891).

tete-a-tete.x: "a private meeting or interview of two persons," 1690s, from French tête-à-tête, literally "head-to-head," thus "face-to-face, in private," from Old French teste "head" (see tete). The adjective use in English, "private, confidential, with none present but the persons concerned" is recorded from 1728; as an adverb in English it dates from 1790.

thalassemia.x: in medicine, a hereditary type of anemia, from thalasso- "sea" + combining form from Greek haima "blood" (see -emia).

thaumaturgy.x: "wonder-working, act of performing something marvelous," 1727, from Greek thaumatourgia, from thaumatourgos (see thaumaturge).

theophagous.x:
"god-eating," 1824; see theo- + -phagous.
 Nicodemus asked our Saviour "how can these things be?" and his divine instructor heard and answered him with complacency : put the same question on any subject of doubt to a theophagous pope from some mountain monastery or some suburban lane, and the fellow will illuminate you with a cartful of faggots. [Landor, "Imaginary Conversations" (Isaac Casaubon speaks), 1824]

thereabouts.x:
early 15c., ther-aboutes, "in that area, near to that place, in that vicinity;" mid-15c., "near to that time, approximately thence," with adverbial -s (see 's) + Middle English ther-aboute, in the same sense, from Old English þær onbutan "about that place;" see there + about.
As "near to that number, quality, or degree" from 1560s. Thereabouts is used of time as well as place, but thenabouts "at about that time" is attested from 1580s. Also in Middle English ther-boute "in the area" (mid-13c.), and Old English had þær neah "nearby it."

therebefore.x: Middle English ther-bifore, from later Old English þær-beforan "in front of them;" see there + before.

thermograph.x: "automatic self-registering thermometer," 1881, from thermo- "temperature, heat" + -graph "instrument for recording; something written." Earlier "a figure produced by action of heat" (1840). Related: Thermographic.

thingamajig.x:
also thingumajig, 1824, an arbitrary extension of thing (n.), used in reference to what the speaker is unable or unwilling to name or specify. Thing (n.) itself was used from 12c. as a generic or meaningless word in place of another or unknown word.
Compare in similar sense kickumbob (1620s); thingum (1680s), thingum-thangum (1670s), thingumbob (1751), thingummy (1796); also sometimes thingamy, thingummarie, thing-a-merry; also jigamaree (1824); such-a-thing (1756). Goldsmith has whangam for an imaginary animal.

thoughtless.x: "wanting thought," in various senses; 1590s, "heedless, imprudent, done without thought," from thought + -less. It is attested by 1680s as "dull-witted." The meaning "inconsiderate of others" is perhaps from 1794. Related: Thoughtlessly; thoughtlessness.

thunderbird.x: legendary cause of thunder (by the flapping of its wings) in some Native American cultures, 1848, a translation of native words, such as Ojibwa (Algonquian) aninikii, Lakotah (Siouan) wakiya, Klamath /lmelmnis/. See thunder (n.) + bird (n.1). In Lakhota, "the thunderbirds call" is "the usual expression for thunder" [Bright].

thunderclap.x: also thunder-clap, late 14c., thonder-clappe, "loud noise of thunder," from thunder (n.) + clap (n.1). Also in the same sense thunder-blast (c. 1300); thunder-crack (15c.), thunder-dint (14c.), thunder-peal (1804).

thunderhead.x: "round, compact, swelling cumulus cloud of the type likely to develop into a thunderstorm," 1861, from thunder (n.) + head (n.). Thunder-cloud is attested from 1690s.

ticky-tacky.x: "inferior, cheap material," 1962, in the song "Little Boxes" by U.S. political folk-singer Malvina Reynolds (1900-1978), a reduplication of tacky. As an adjective by 1967.

tiddlywinks.x: children's tile-flipping game, 1857, probably an arbitrary formation in baby talk, but there was a slang tiddly-wink "unlicensed drink shop" (1844), from slang tiddly "a drink; drunk."

tight-assed.x: "unable or unwilling to relax," by 1903, colloquial; see tight (adj.) + ass (n.2). Tight-ass (n.) in reference to an uptight person is by 1972.

tilly-vally.x: an old exclamation of impatience, "bosh! nonsense!" 1520s, of unknown origin, perhaps arbitrary. Used by Skelton and Shakespeare.

time-keeper.x: also timekeeper, 1680s, "scientific instrument for regulating the passage of time, chronometer;" see time (n.) + keeper. By 1795 as "one who marks, measures, or records time." To keep time is by 1590s of musicians, 1899 of watches.

tobacconist.x:
"dealer in tobacco," 1650s, from tobacco + -ist + abnormal inserted consonant, perhaps on the model of Latinate pattern in words such as Platonist.
The earlier meaning was "smoker, person addicted to tobacco" (1590s), now obsolete. Tobacchian (also obsolete) also was used in this sense. Tobaccanalian (1835) was a humorous or nonce word.

tongue-lash.x: "scold, abuse with words," 1857, from tongue (n.) + lash (v.). Related: Tongue-lashing (n.) "a scolding, wordy vituperation." Also compare 19c. slang tongue-bang (v.) "scold heartily;" tongue-banger "scold;" also Australian slang ear-bash (v.) "talk inordinately" to someone (1944).

tonsillitis.x: also tonsilitis, "inflammation of the tonsils," 1801, from combining form of tonsil + -itis "inflammation." Related: Tonsillitic, tonsilitic (adj.), which however also can mean "of or pertaining to the tonsils."

topsy-turvy.x:
1520s, "but prob. in popular use from an earlier period" [OED, 1989]; likely from tops, plural of top (n.1) "highest point" + obsolete terve "turn upside down, topple over" (compare top over terve "to fall over," mid-15c.). As an adjective from 1610s.
Middle English terven "throw down, toss, reverse, turn upside down," is from Old English tearflian "to roll over, overturn," from Proto-Germanic *terbanan (source also of Old High German zerben "to turn round").
Century Dictionary calls topsy-turvy "A word which, owing to its popular nature, its alliterative type, and to ignorance of its origin, leading to various perversions made to suggest some plausible origin, has undergone, besides the usual variations of spelling, extraordinary modifications of form." It lists and dates 31 variations.
There were earlier similar expressions in nautical use, from the "upper part of a ship's mast" sense of top (n.1), such as topsails over "head over heels" (c. 1400).
Related: Topsy-turvydom; topsy-turvyism; topsy-turvyfication; topsy-turvyfy.

totipalmate.x: "having all the toes fully webbed," 1872, from Latin toti-, combining form of totus "whole, all" (see total (adj.)) + palma "palm" (of the hand); see palm (n.1) + -ate (1).

townspeople.x: "people of a town," 1640s, from genitive of town (n.) + people (n.). Town people "the sort of people who live in towns" is by 1887. Townfolk "people who live in towns" is from c. 1300 (toun folc). Townsman is from Old English as "villein, tenant farmer;" early 15c. as "citizen of a town;" c. 1600 as "fellow citizen." Middle English also had tounman (Old English tun-mann "villein"), attested by late 14c, as "town dweller, townsman, inhabitant of a town."

trailblazer.x: by 1893, "one who makes a path for others to follow," typically figurative, from trail (n.) + agent noun from blaze (v.3) "mark" a tree or trail.

transalpine.x: also trans-alpine, 1580s, "being or situated beyond the Alps" (originally and usually as viewed from Rome); see trans- + Alpine.

transceiver.x: 1934, the word like the thing a combination of transmitter and receiver.

transfixion.x: "act of piercing through, state of being pierced through," literal or figurative, c. 1600, noun of action from transfix (v.). In surgery, as a process in amputation, by 1872, also transfixation (1889).

translatese.x: "style of language considered typical of translators," usually derogatory, by 1967; see translate + -ese. Earlier was translationese (1957).

transnormal.x: also trans-normal, "exceeding or beyond what is normal, abnormal by excess," 1853; see trans- + normal (adj.).

transponder.x: "unit which receives and automatically responds," 1945, from trans(mit) + (res)pond + agent noun suffix -er (1).

transracial.x: "across racial boundaries," by 1925, American English; see trans- + racial.

transversal.x: "running or lying across, placed across," mid-15c., from Medieval Latin transversalis (13c.), from transvers-, stem of transvertere (see transverse). Earlier in the same sense was transversary (c. 1400). As a noun, from 1590s in geometry, "a line drawn across several others so as to touch them all." Related: Transversally.

trapezoidal.x: "having the form of a trapezoid," 1796, from trapezoid + -al (1). "Having the form of a trapezium" is properly trapeziform (1776).

treasonable.x: "of or pertaining to treason, involving or partaking of treason," late 14c., from treason + -able. Related: Treasonably; treasonableness.

trendsetter.x: also trend-setter, "one who or that which establishes or advances trends in style, opinion, etc.," 1950, from trend (n.) + agent noun from set (v.). Related: Trend-setting. Trend-spotter "one who observes and seeks to predict popular trends in style, opinion, etc." is by 1965.

trisyllable.x: "a three-syllable word," 1580s; see tri- "three" + syllable (n.). Related: Trisyllabic.

trusteeship.x:
"office or function of a trustee," 1730; see trustee + -ship.
 Such a word as 
 trusteeship is eminently characteristic of the composite character of the language: Scandinavian 
 trust + a French ending used in a manner unparalleled in French + an Old English ending. [Otto Jespersen, "Growth and Structure of the English Language"]

tuberculous.x: 1747, "characterized by tubers," from Latin tuberculum (see tubercle) + -ous. By 1882 as "characterized by tuberculosis."

tulipomania.x: "craze for the cultivation or buying of tulip bulbs," especially that raging among all classes in Holland in 1630s, in which many were ruined; 1710, from tulip + mania, with connective vowel, and compare French tulipomane. The Dutch term was tulpenhandel. Related: Tulipomaniac.

twelvemonth.x: also twelve-month, "a year, period of 12 months," Old English twelf-monð; see twelve + month.

typographer.x: "printer, one skilled in typography," 1640s, from typography + -er (1). A typographist (1851) is a student of typography; one versed in the history or art of printing.

typographic.x: 1778, "of or pertaining to the art of printing from types," from Medieval Latin typographicus (16c.), from typographus, from Greek typos (see type (n.)) + graphos "writing," from graphein "to write" (see -graphy).

tyrannicide.x: 1640s, "act of killing a tyrant;" 1650s, "one who kills a tyrant;" from combining form of Greek tyrannos (see tyranno-) + -cide.

Thurberesque.x: "of or in the style of U.S. writer and illustrator James Thurber" (1894-1961), noted for short, humorous observations on domestic life, by 1954.

technicality.x: 1814, "that which is peculiar to any science, art, etc.," from technical + -ity. The meaning "technical character or quality" is from 1828. Related: Technicalities.

telaesthesia.x: "telepathy, perception at a distance," 1882, a word in Latin form from Greek elements; for first, see tele-; second is from Greek aisthēsis "feeling" (from PIE root *au- "to perceive"). For the abstract noun ending, see -ia.

telegraphese.x: "severely condensed form of English (omitting articles, pronouns, auxiliary verbs, etc.) used to save expenses in writing telegraphs," which charged by the word, 1885, from telegraph (n.) + -ese. In early use sometimes also in jocular reference to the writing style in the London "Daily Telegraph," which was rather the reverse. Also compare cablese.

temporaneous.x: 1650s, "lasting for a time only, temporary;" also 1650s as "pertaining to time, temporal," from Late Latin temporaneous "timely." from Latin tempus (genitive temporis) "time, season; proper time" (see temporal (adj.1)).

tessellation.x: 1650s, "minute arrangement of parts or colors," noun of action from Late Latin tessellatus "made of small, square stones or tiles" (see tessellated). By 1813 as "act or art of making inlaid work."

testosterone.x: male sex hormone, 1935, from German Testosteron (1935), coined from a presumed combining form of Latin testis "testicle" (see testis) + first syllable of sterol + chemical ending -one.

therebetween.x: c. 1400, ther-bitwene, "between the two, between two objects or points in time;" see there + between.

therethrough.x: late Old English, ther-thurgh, "all the way through, in and out of it, from one side to the other;" see there + through. In early use therethorough; form therethrough is by 1590s.

thermocouple.x: also thermo-couple, device for measuring temperature, 1862, short for thermoelectric couple; see thermo- + electric + couple (n.).

thermography.x: "heat-drawing; method of writing which requires heat to develop the characters," 1840, from thermo- "temperature, heat" + -graphy. In reference to processes using infrared radiation, by 1967.

thermosphere.x: part of the upper atmosphere where air density is chiefly controlled by temperature, 1924, from thermo- "temperature, heat" + -sphere (n.), an element abstracted from atmosphere (n.)

thoroughbred.x:
1701, of persons, "thoroughly accomplished," from thorough + past tense of breed.
It is regarded as a figurative extension of the phrase in reference to horses, "of pure breed or stock," but it is attested earlier of persons. Of animals, it is used 1729 in The Caledonian Mercury (Feb. 3) of a bull advertised for sale in Gilmerton Parks, and the term is used by 1731 in English and Scottish newspaper advertisements of horses.
 Now put the case, here are two mares, both originally bred from Arabian horses, and mares, or the descendants of such, which I suppose is all that is to be understood by the term of thorough-bred horses (etc.) [W. Osmer, "Treatise on the Diseases and Lameness of Horses," 1766] 
But print references in the first half of the 18c. typically are to persons: a thorough-bred seaman (often), artist, courtier, connoisseur, scholar, cook, and it was used once of flax.
Hence, "having the qualities characteristic of pure breeding; high-spirited elegance in form or bearing." As a noun by 1842, "animal of pure stock."

thoroughfare.x: late 14c., thurgh-fare, "passage or way through," also "way-station," from thorough (before it had differentiated from through) + fare (n.) "journey, road." The notion is "that through which ones goes (fares)."

thunderstorm.x: also thunder-storm, "storm accompanied by thunder and lightning," 1560s, from thunder (n.) + storm (n.). The less severe thunder-shower is attested from 1690s.

time-honored.x: also time-honoured, "venerable by reason of antiquity," 1590s; from time (n.) + past participle of honor (v.).

time-sharing.x: 1953, as a computing term, from time (n.) + verbal noun from share (v.). In real estate, as an arrangement in property use, it is recorded from 1976. Related: Time-share (n.).

togetherness.x: 1650s, "state of being together," from together + -ness. Sense of "fellowship, fellow-feeling," is from 1930.

tonsillolith.x: "concretion in a tonsil," 1894, from tonsillo-, combining form of tonsil + -lith "stone."

totalitarian.x:
1926, in reference to Italian fascism, "of or pertaining to a system of government which tolerates but one political party, to which all other institutions and all individuals are subordinated;" a word formed in English on the model of Italian totalitario ("complete, absolute; totalitarian") from total (adj.) + ending from authoritarian.
The noun is recorded from 1938, "member of a party advocating totalitarian principles." Totalist (n.) was used (especially in sociology) in the sense of "one inclined to treat things as a whole."

toxicophobia.x: "morbid fear of being poisoned," 1876, from toxico- "poison" (see toxic (adj.)) + -phobia. Related: Toxicophobiac.

tracheostomy.x: "operation of making an opening in the trachea," 1945, from tracheo-, combining form of trachea + -ostomy "artificial opening," (see ostomy).

tranquilizer.x: 1800, "one who or that which tranquilizes" (oldest in an extended sense in reference to a ruffian gang); from 1824 as "a sedative substance" (the earliest reference is to ground ivy), agent noun from tranquilize. In reference to one of a large group of anti-anxiety drugs, by 1956.

transcendent.x:
mid-15c., "pre-eminent, surpassing, extraordinary," from Latin transcendentem (nominative transcendens) "surmounting, rising above," present participle of transcendere (see transcend).
In Scholastic philosophy, "not included under (higher than) one of Aristotle's 10 categories" (by c. 1300 in Medieval Latin). In reference to Kant and later his followers, by 1803. In modern theology, "transcending the universe of matter," by 1877. Also sometimes transcendant. Related: Transcendently.

transduction.x: "act of leading or carrying over," 1650s, from Latin transductionem/traducionem (nominative transductio) "a removal, transfer," noun of action from past-participle stem of transducere/traducere "change over, convert," also "lead in parade, make a show of, dishonor, disgrace," originally "lead along or across, bring through, transfer" (see traduce). With specialized senses in 20c. Related: Transductor.

transferable.x: also transferrable, "capable of being transferred or conveyed from one place or person to another; capable of being legitimately passed into the ownership of another," 1650s, from transfer (v.) + -able.

transference.x: "act of transferring," 1680s; see transfer (v.) + -ence. In psychoanalytical sense it is recorded from 1911, translating German übertragung (Freud). Related: Transferential.

translatable.x: "that may be rendered into another language," 1745; see translate + -able. Related: Translatability.

transmontane.x: also trans-montane, "across or beyond a mountain or mountains," 1727, from Latin transmontanus, from trans "over, beyond" (see trans-) + montanus (see mountain).

transmutable.x: "capable of being changed into a different substance," late 15c., from Medieval Latin transmutabilis, from past-participle stem of Latin transmutare "change from one condition to another" (see transmute). Related: Transmutably; transmutability.

transposable.x: "that may be transposed" in any sense, 1835; see transpose (v.) + -able. Transponible is attested by 1891 as "capable of being transposed without violation of an assumed condition."

transumption.x:
early 15c., transumpcioun, "copying, transcription, passage copied," from Old French transumption and directly from Latin trans(s)umptionem (nominative trans(s)umptio) "a taking of one thing from another," noun of action from past-participle stem of trans(s)umere "to take" from one to another, "adopt, assume," from trans "over, across" (see trans-) + sumere "to take, obtain, buy," from sus‑, variant of sub‑ "up from under" (see sub-) + emere "to take" (from PIE root *em- "to take, distribute").
In rhetoric, "a metaphor or simile," mid-15c. Related: Transumptive. Middle English also had transumpt (adj.) "adopted, taken over," in reference to words used figuratively, from the Latin past-participle.

transvection.x: "act of conveying or carrying over," 1610s, from Latin transvectionem (nominative transvectio) "act of carrying across or over," from trans (see trans-) + past-participle stem of vehere "to carry" (see vehicle).

trichromatic.x: "having or relating to three fundamental colors," 1891; see tri- "three" + chromatic (adj.). Related: Trichromatism (1854).

triglyceride.x: 1860, irregularly formed in chemistry from tri- + glycerine + ide. So called for the three radicals which replace the three hydrogen atoms.

troublemaker.x: also trouble-maker, "one who makes disorder, agitation, or disturbance," 1843, from trouble (n.) + maker. Earlier was troubler "quarrelsome or contentious person" (late 14c.), stroublere "perturbator, one who disturbs proper order," from Old French troubleur, variant of torbleor.

twitterpated.x:
1942, apparently first attested in the Walt Disney movie "Bambi" (there also was a song by that name but it was not in the studio release of the film), a past-participle adjective formed from twitter in the "tremulous excitement" noun sense (1670s) + pate (n.2) "head" (compare flutterpated, 1894).
 Flower, Bambi, Thumper: Twitterpated? 
 Friend Owl: Yes. Nearly everybody gets twitterpated in the springtime. For example: You're walking along, minding your own business. You're looking neither to the left, nor to the right, when all of a sudden you run smack into a pretty face. Woo-woo! You begin to get weak in the knees. Your head's in a whirl. And then you feel light as a feather, and before you know it, you're walking on air. And then you know what? You're knocked for a loop, and you completely lose your head! 
 Thumper: Gosh, that's awful.

type-setting.x: also typesetting, "act or art of setting or combining types in order for printing," 1824, from type (n.) in the printing sense + verbal noun from set (v.).

Theophrastian.x: 1660s, "of or pertaining to Theophrastus," the Greek philosopher, especially in reference to his 30 sketches "on disagreeable aspects of human behavior" [OED, 1989].

Tupperware.x:
trademark (reg. U.S.) for a line of plastic containers, sold to potential buyers at "parties" held by invitation in private homes; popular from 1947; the name is from ware (n.) + Earl S. Tupper, New England chemist and inventor, who set up Tupperware Corp. but did not see success until after wartime restrictions ended.
 At his big-windowed brick factory in Farnumsville, Mass., orders for Tupperware were pouring in — from the American Thermos Bottle Co. for 7,000,000 nesting cups; from Canada Dry Ginger Ale for 50,000 bowls to sell with beverages; from Tek Corp. for 50,000 tumblers to sell with toothbrushes; from Camel for 300,000 cigaret cases. To top it off, Manhattan’s Museum of Modern Art would include two of Tupper’s bowls in a forthcoming show of useful objects. ["Time" magazine, Sept. 8, 1947] 
 What is Tupperware? It's a new wonder plastic (Poly-T) molded into glasses, pitchers, bowls. It looks as fragile, as delicate as alabaster, mother of pearl. Hold a Tupperware tumbler to the light—it's translucent, opalescent. Throw it against the wall, step on it, crush it—it bounces right back into shape. [advertisement, "Buffalo News," Jan. 14, 1948, and other U.S. newspapers]

teeter-totter.x: "a see-saw," 1871, from teeter (v.); earlier simply teeter (1855), and titter-totter (n.) in same sense is attested from 1520s (as a verb by 1825). An earlier name for it was merry-totter (mid-15c.); Cotgrave's dictionary (1611) has totter-arse. The modern word is perhaps a reduplication, but totter (n.) "board swing, see-saw" is recorded from late 14c. (see totter (v.)). Also compare see-saw.

telecommuting.x: by 1975, as a hypothetical arrangement where an office job is done from home by means of electrical equipment; verbal noun from telecommute. It is said to have been coined by Jack Niles of USC.

teleportation.x: 1931 as a term in psychics; by 1951 in science fiction; from tele- + ending of transportation. Apparently coined by Charles Fort (1874-1932).

televangelist.x: "evangelist preacher with a television program," 1973, from tele(vision) + evangelist. Earliest usages are in reference to Rex Humbard (1919-2007). Television evangelist is attested from 1958.

temperamental.x: 1640s, "of or pertaining to temperament," from temperament + -al (1); in the sense of "moody, having an erratic temper" it is recorded by 1907. Related: Temperamentally.

tenebrescence.x: loosely, "a tending to grow dark," coined 1946, in "Luminescence and Tenebrescence as Applied to Radar" [H.W. Leverenz in "RCA Review," vol. vii, no. 2, June], which defines it as "any absorption of light not intrinsic to the materials involved," and explains: "The terms 'tenebrescence' and 'scotophor' are derived from Latin and Greek sources to correspond to the terms 'luminescence' and 'phosphor.' "

terpsichorean.x: "pertaining to dancing," 1869, literally "of Terpsichore," from Latinized form of Greek Terpsikhorē, muse of choral dance and the dramatic chorus (see Terpsichore). As a noun, "a female dancer," by 1889. Hence theatrical slang shortening terp "stage dancer, chorus girl" (1937).

terriculament.x: "a cause of terror," especially "object of needless dread, bugbear," 1540s, now obsolete, from Late Latin terriculamentum "something to excite terror," from terrere "fill with fear" (see terrible).

terrorization.x: also terrorisation, "act of terrorizing; state of being terrorized," by 1868, noun of action from terrorize (v.). In early use in U.S. in referenced to Kansas in 1856, the presidential campaign of 1876.

thanatography.x: "a narration of one's death," 1839 (Thackeray); see thanato- "death" + -graphy "a description of."

thenceforward.x: "from that time or place onward," mid-15c., from thence + forward. Related: Thenceforwards.

thermodynamic.x: "caused or operated by force due to application of heat," 1849, from thermo- "temperature, heat" + dynamic (adj.). Related: Thermodynamical; thermodynamically.

thermonuclear.x: in reference to nuclear reactions occurring only at very high temperatures, 1938 in astrophysics, of stars; by 1953 of weapons (technically only to describe the hydrogen bomb); from thermo- "temperature, heat" + nuclear (adj.).

thick-skinned.x: 1540s, "one who or that which has thick skin or rind;" see thick (adj.) + skin (n.). The figurative use is by c. 1600, originally "dull of sensation or feeling," by early 19c. especially "insensible or not easily irritated by taunts and ridicule."

thigmotropism.x: "movement of an organism toward or away from contact with a foreign body," 1900, with tropism + thigmo-, combining form meaning "touch," from Greek thigma "touch" from thinganein "touch with the hands; occupy oneself with," which is reconstructed in Watkins to be from PIE root *dheigh- "to form, build."

thoroughgoing.x: "out-and-out, complete, doing things all the way," 1800, from thorough (q.v.) + going. Middle English had a verb thorough-go or through-go (thurhgon) "to go through," from Old English þurhgangan.

tick-tack-toe.x:
children's three-in-a-row game with Xs and Os, so called by 1892, earlier tit-tat-toe (by 1852, in reminiscences of earlier years), also called noughts and crosses (1852), also oughts and crosses. Probably from the sound of the pencil on the slate with which it originally was played by schoolboys.
Also the name of a children's counting rhyme played on slate (also originally tit-tat-toe, by 1842), and compare tick-tack (1580s), a form of backgammon, possibly from French trictrac, perhaps imitative of the sound of tiles on the board.
